title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text: Early- and late-Universe measurements of the Hubble constant disagree, a puzzle known as the Hubble tension. We derive cosmological parameters from first principles, using only the dynamics of cosmic volume and the possibility that matter can be unevenly distributed. Within this framework, three of the six parameters of the standard model are obtained from the underlying dynamics rather than fitted to observations: volume formation determines the dark-energy density parameter to be two thirds, spatial curvature vanishes, and the matter density follows from the remaining cosmic energy budget. The Hubble constant remains an observational input because it represents a calendar date rather than an intrinsic property of the Universe, while the two remaining parameters are likewise taken from observation. Once cosmic unevenness is included as a dynamical component, both the expansion rate and the dark-energy density parameter become redshift dependent. The latter increases by eight percent toward the present, from 0.679 in the homogeneous early Universe to 0.735 today, consistent with independent probes spanning several orders of magnitude in redshift, including the microwave background, supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, X-ray clusters and gravitational waves. This same mechanism yields the time-evolving dark energy favored by recent combined analyses without introducing a new free parameter. Integrating the resulting expansion history gives a cosmic age of 13.521 Gyr, shorter than the homogeneous value by 0.306 Gyr. This difference is a global time dilation: dark energy and time evolve together, shaped by the unevenness of the cosmos.

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
section: THE HUBBLE TENSION AND THE DYNAMICS OF THE UNIVERSE
text:
The Hubble tension, the discrepancy between earlyand late-Universe determinations of the Hubble constant H0, has become one of the central problems of contemporary cosmology. Its implications reach beyond a single parameter: if H0 is not strictly constant, the Hubble time tH = H−1

0 , which underlies the inferred age and temporal evolution of the Universe, must also be reconsidered. Because H0 is moreover tied to the expansion dynamics, and hence to the dark-energy density parameter ΩΛ, any reassessment of H0 entails a parallel re-evaluation of dark energy.

The present work re-examines cosmic time and dark energy jointly, based on the volume dynamics (VD) of space [1, 2]. A central feature of the VD is that it does not require the real Universe to be exactly homogeneous: the homogeneity assumed in the standard ΛCDM model does not hold on all scales [3, 4], so that quantities inferred under that assumption, including the commonly quoted cosmic age of ≈13.8 Gyr, are idealized. The dynamical influence of such inhomogeneity on cosmological averages has been studied extensively within general

The remaining parameters are taken from observation. The Hubble constant H0,ΛCDM represents a calendar date tH0 = 1/H0, the epoch at which we happen to observe the Universe. Therefore, it cannot be derived from first principles; it must be obtained with the help of a measurement. Density parameters, being ratios to the critical density, are free of that calibration, whereas absolute densities such as ρΛ = ΩΛ ρcr. inherit the epoch of observation through ρcr. = 3H2

0/(8πG); the ratios are therefore what the present derivations provide. The parameter σ8 is measured. The density parameter of radiation follows from the measured redshift zeq of matter-radiation equality: since ρm ∝(1 + z)3 and ρr ∝(1 + z)4, equality implies Ωr = Ωm/(1+zeq), which converges after a single iteration started from Ωm ≈1/3; here Ωr comprises photons and relativistic neutrinos, as in the determination of zeq [11].

text:
Physics before the classical Big Bang. As a consequence of gravity and quantum physics, the density in nature is bounded by one half of the Planck density, ρP /2 with ρP = 5.155 × 1096 kg/m3. At a time t1 in the past, the Universe reached ρ1 ≈ρP /2, with a present-day light horizon as small as R1 ≈8.2×10−6 m [22], still far above the Planck length LP = 1.616 × 10−35 m. The Big Bang is therefore completed by the physics before the classical Big Bang (BCBB) [1, 22]: indivisible volume portions exhibit p = D −1 transverse modes and can thus span D-dimensional space, so the BCBB started at D ≈301, R ≈LP and ρ ≈ρP /2; expansion and consecutive dimensional phase transitions unfolded the cosmos until the state at R1 and D = 3 was reached, whereupon the classical Big Bang followed. Both processes have been modeled in a computer simulation [1, 22]. In particular, the horizon and flatness problems, commonly addressed by cosmic inflation [23], are thereby solved from first principles [20]. Moreover, the states at D ≥3 provide an excitation spectrum of space, from which the formation of neutrinos can be treated.

Altogether, among the six cosmological parameters, H0,ΛCDM represents a calendar date and must therefore be measured. Of the remaining five, three are derived here rather than fitted, and they agree with observation within the stated uncertainties. A derivation of σ8 and of the radiation content from the physics before the classical Big Bang, based on the excitation spectrum of volume portions and the formation of neutrinos [1, 22], is the subject of a forthcoming publication.

VALIDATION

The derived density parameter of dark energy in the heterogeneous Universe,

ΩΛ,het(z) = Ωvol (1 + κ(z))ξ(z)

Ωm + Ωvol (1 + κ(z))ξ(z) ,

with the measured CMB value Ωvol = 0.679 used in place of the theoretical value 2/3 (Appendix E) and Ωm = 0.321 [11], increases monotonically as the redshift decreases: from ΩΛ,het ≈0.679 at high redshift (the homogeneous early Universe) toward 0.735 ± 0.010 near z = 0. The full evolution is shown in Fig. 1.

As an empirical test, the predicted curve is compared in Fig. 1 with literature values that span several orders of magnitude in redshift and originate from mutually independent methods (CMB analyses, baryon acoustic oscillations, gravitational-wave catalogs, type Ia supernova compilations, X-ray cluster abundances and galaxy/quasar observations). In particular, the lowredshift value ΩΛ,het(z = 0) = 0.735 ± 0.010 agrees with independent determinations [24, 25], while the highprecision Planck value (z ≈1000, ΩΛ = 0.679 ± 0.013) [11] fixes the high-redshift end of the curve rather than testing it, as discussed below. The remaining points likewise lie close to the prediction, their deviations being consistent with the differing methods and uncertainties; the complete list of literature values is given in Table I. This broad agreement across the observed redshift range supports the physical relevance of the heterogeneous darkenergy model.

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text:
The literature values entering this comparison require a remark on their interpretation. Each of them is an effective parameter, inferred from the data of a given redshift range under the assumption of a homogeneous background, and each is shown at the mean redshift of the underlying probe. They are therefore not determinations of an instantaneous ΩΛ(z), and Fig. 1 is not a pointby-point measurement of the derived function. The same reading underlies published analyses in which the Hubble constant is inferred separately in redshift bins and a trend with redshift is reported [26, 27]: within each bin the parameter is treated as constant, while the collection of bins is examined for evolution. If the parameters are in fact redshift dependent, an analysis of this kind returns an average over the interval it covers rather than a local value, so that the effective values are expected to follow the derived curve without coinciding with it exactly. The gray horizontal bars in Figs. 1 and 2 indicate the intervals over which each average is taken. These two analyses, and the functions they fit to their binned values, are examined in Sec. VI.

A further qualification concerns the high-redshift end of both curves. There the heterogeneity vanishes, κ(z) → 0, so that ΩΛ,het →Ωvol and H0,het →H0,ΛCDM, and the curves approach the measured input values, Ωvol = 0.679 in Fig. 1 and H0,ΛCDM = 66.88 km s−1 Mpc−1 in Fig. 2.

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text: That derivation belongs to the first of three stages of modeling, and keeping the stages apart prevents a misunderstanding that the notation invites. (i) Volume formation is analyzed in empty space and yields the darkenergy density ρvol, hence Ωvol = 2/3. Empty space contains nothing that could be diluted by the expansion, so no density evolves in time at this stage, and the Hubble time tH0 is defined while an age of the Universe is not. (ii) Homogeneous matter and radiation are then placed in the formed space, which gives the ΛCDM model; only here does the integrated expansion history yield an age, because Ωm and Ωr enter the integrand. (iii) Heterogeneity is added last, as developed in this work. Stages (ii) and (iii) express their results as ratios with respect to the stage before, ΩΛ,het/Ωvol, H0,het(z)/H0,ΛCDM and tU,het/tU,hom, so that the result of the preceding stage is used but never reopened. Reading the relation ρΛ = ΩΛ ρcr. across the stages would suggest that ρvol falls as the critical density falls. It does not: within stage (i) there is no time evolution of any density, and the later stages modify that result by the stated ratios rather than recomputing it. The relation from which ρvol follows, equation (E19), connects the rate of volume formation with ρvol and the Hubble time alone, and dividing by the critical density removes the epoch of observation and leaves the pure number 2/3, equation (E22). The epoch dependence of absolute densities noted in Sec. III therefore concerns their calibration against a measured H0, not an evolution within stage (i).

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text:
A limitation of this test should be stated openly. The comparison confronts the derived functions with cosmological parameters as published by the respective analyses, not with the underlying data sets themselves. No likelihood analysis of supernova magnitudes, baryon acoustic oscillation distances or cluster counts against the heterogeneous model has been carried out, so the agreement seen in Figs. 1 and 2 is not a goodness-offit statement. Two considerations motivate this choice. First, apart from the measured inputs that fix the highredshift end, the derived functions contain no parameter that is adjusted to the data entering the comparison, so what is shown is a test of a prediction and not a fit; in particular, the evolution toward low redshift follows from the derivation and is not tuned to the values it is compared with. Second, a joint reanalysis of the underlying catalogs would require the full covariance structure of each sample together with a consistent treatment of the calibration and nuisance parameters of each method, which lies beyond the scope of this work. Such a direct confrontation, in particular with the supernova Hubble

diagram itself, is left for future work.

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text:
OF GLOBAL TIME DILATION

A. Motivation and Approach

While the standard ΛCDM framework assumes a homogeneous universe with constant density parameters, the results above show that this is an idealization: in a realistic, heterogeneous universe the Hubble parameter H, the Hubble constant H0 and the dark-energy density parameter ΩΛ evolve with redshift because of structure formation, including the formation of heterogeneity. The temporal evolution of the Universe must therefore be reconsidered, and the age is derived below as a function of redshift, allowing a direct comparison between the homogeneous and the heterogeneous model.

The age tU(z) of the Universe is obtained, for both the homogeneous and the heterogeneous case, by integrating the relation between the scale factor and cosmic time, with the redshift-dependent H0,het(z) and ΩΛ,het(z) derived above entering the integrand. The full integral, the auxiliary functions κ(z) and ξ(z), and the numerical scheme are given in Appendix E.

B. Age Difference and Time Dilation

Evaluating the integrated expansion history numerically for the present day, x2 = 1 =: x0, gives the presentday age of the heterogeneous Universe

tU,het(x0) = 13.521+0.355

−0.338 Gyr. (5)

The corresponding age of the homogeneous Universe, obtained by replacing ΩΛ,het with Ωvol = ΩΛ,hom and Ωm,het with Ωm, is

tU,hom(x0) = 13.827+0.357

−0.340 Gyr. (6)

The time difference ∆tU = tU,hom −tU,het, equation (E38), represents a global time dilation of the homogeneous Universe: between the same two events, the homogeneous Universe exhibits a larger time interval than the heterogeneous Universe.

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text:
ANALYSES OF H0

That the Hubble constant inferred from observations is not constant across redshift was reported before the present work. Krishnan et al. [26] found a descending trend in a combined low-redshift data set, and Dainotti et al. [27] found the same behavior in the Pantheon supernova compilation. Both results are empirical: the values obtained in the individual bins are fitted with a function chosen for convenience, and the trend is read off from its parameters. The present work builds on these findings. What those analyses established for a limited range of redshift follows here from a derivation, and it extends to the full range up to the microwave background. The two fitted functions are shown together with the derived H0,het(z) in Fig. 2.

A. The descending line of Krishnan et al.

Krishnan et al. [26] bin megamasers, cosmic chronometers, type Ia supernovae and baryon acoustic oscillations at z ≤0.7 into six bins and fit the flat ΛCDM model separately in each. The resulting values of H0 descend with redshift, and a weighted straight-line fit gives a slope of −21.7 ± 9.4 km s−1 Mpc−1 per unit redshift with an intercept of 73.6 ± 2.5 km s−1 Mpc−1, the slope differing from a horizontal line at 2.1σ. The intercept is an outcome of that fit rather than an input, and it agrees with the present-day value of the derived function, H0,het(0) = 73.6 km s−1 Mpc−1. Over the fitted interval the derived function descends more slowly: its mean slope between z = 0 and z = 0.61 is −7.7 km s−1 Mpc−1 per unit redshift, which lies 1.5 standard deviations from the fitted slope.

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text:
A straight line cannot, however, describe the behavior outside the interval in which it was obtained. Continued to higher redshift it reaches H0 = 0 at z ≈3.4 and turns negative beyond. As the zero is approached the Hubble

9

time tH = 1/H0 diverges, so that the implied age of the Universe grows without bound, which the cosmic-clock constraint of Tomasetti et al. [41] excludes. The line is therefore a local approximation to the measured trend, valid where it was fitted, and the feature it identifies calls for a function that also possesses a high-redshift limit. The derived H0,het(z) provides one: as the heterogeneity vanishes, κ(z) →0, the function approaches the value measured at the microwave background.

B. The evolutionary parameterization of Dainotti

et al.

Dainotti et al. [27] divide the Pantheon compilation of 1048 supernovae into 3, 4, 20 and 40 redshift bins and fit the extracted values with H0(z) = ˜H0(1 + z)−α. For three bins in the flat ΛCDM model they obtain

˜H0 = 73.577±0.106 km s−1 Mpc−1 and α = 0.009±0.004, the evolutionary parameter differing from zero at 2.0σ; the other binnings give values consistent with these. Here

˜H0 is not an independent determination, because the absolute magnitude of the supernovae is calibrated so that H0 = 73.5 km s−1 Mpc−1 at z = 0. The informative quantity is the exponent, and it confirms the descending trend.

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text:
With an exponent of order 10−2 the function falls very slowly. Extrapolated to the last scattering surface it yields 69.2 ± 2.2 km s−1 Mpc−1, which remains above the measured 66.88±0.92 km s−1 Mpc−1 [11]; the compatibility reported by the authors rests on the large uncertainty propagated from α. The shape differs as well, as Fig. 2 shows. A power law of this kind carries no characteristic redshift and therefore stays close to its present-day value throughout, whereas the determinations of Table II and the derived function fall from the local range toward the microwave-background value between z ≈0.01 and z ≈3. The derived function reproduces that behavior because the heterogeneity on which it rests grows as κ(z) ∝(1 + z)−5/2, equation (E33), which fixes both where the transition occurs and where the function levels off.

C. Derivation and parameterization

Both functions were introduced to test whether the binned values are constant, and for that purpose the choice of function is secondary. Neither is derived, and neither relates the trend to a physical cause: a straight line and a power law contain no quantity that links H0(z) to the structure of the Universe. In the present framework the redshift dependence is not assumed. It follows from the law of locally formed volume, equation (E16), with the growth of heterogeneity entering through σ8, so that the shape of the function and its high-redshift limit are fixed before any comparison with data is made. This is what allows a single function to hold from the

microwave background to the present day.

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text:
Recent observational studies aim to constrain the age of the Universe independently of a single cosmological model. A relevant example is provided by Tomasetti et al. [41], who use the ages of the oldest Milky Way stars as cosmic clocks to obtain a lower limit on the age of the Universe, tU ≥13.8 ± 1.0 (stat.) ± 1.4 (syst.) Gyr. Such constraints are usually interpreted within a homogeneous ΛCDM framework, which does not account for the dynamical influence of large-scale heterogeneity on cosmic time. The present work shows that, once heterogeneity is included as a dynamical component, the Hubble parameter, the Hubble constant H0(z) and the dark-energy density parameter ΩΛ(z) become coupled to the time evolution of the Universe. The cosmic age is therefore no longer fixed by the homogeneous expansion history alone, but depends on the model used to describe the real, structured Universe.

Integrating the redshift-dependent expansion history, equation (E31), yields the self-consistent age of the heterogeneous Universe, tU = 13.521+0.355

title: Cosmic Heterogeneity Shapes the Evolution of Dark Energy and Time
text:
−0.338 Gyr, which remains compatible with the cosmic-clock bound, lying within one standard deviation of its central value. This indicates that the cosmic-clock age constraint, the observed discrepancy in H0 [36] and the time evolution of ΩΛ(z) need not be regarded as separate problems, but may be different observational manifestations of the same underlying fact: the Universe is not perfectly homogeneous, and its heterogeneity influences the progression of cosmic time. Together with its agreement with independent empirical constraints, the temporal evolution of dark energy derived here forms a coherent framework linking cosmic structure, dark energy and the age of the Universe. Independent late-Universe analyses point in the same direction: baryon acoustic oscillation measurements of the DESI collaboration favor a time-evolving dark energy when combined with supernova and CMB data [29], and the Hubble diagram of quasars at high redshift suggests a dark-energy density that increases with cosmic time [42] (see also Fig. 1). A more detailed discussion, including the interpretation of tU, H0 and σ8 as effective averaged quantities and an outlook on future tests, is given in Appendix D.

More broadly, the heterogeneous treatment developed here forms part of a first-principles cosmological framework based on the volume dynamics of space [1, 2] (Fig. 4), within which the coupling of cosmic structure, dark energy and cosmic time examined in this work arises naturally.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: We infer the Hubble constant $H_0$ from the ~400 Extragalactic Distance Database hosts with a tip of the red giant branch (TRGB) distance, calibrated on the geometric anchors of the Large Magellanic Cloud and NGC 4258. We forward-model the tip magnitudes and host redshifts including magnitude-limited selection, sky exposure, and density-dependent galaxy bias, conditioning on each of the 80 Manticore-Local realisations of the local density and peculiar-velocity fields in turn. As most hosts lie at $cz_{\rm CMB} \lesssim 1000$ km/s, where peculiar velocities are important, the inference is limited by the variance of these fields rather than by the TRGB calibration. For a fixed realisation, the redshift likelihood and density smoothing each move $H_0$ by less than 1 km/s/Mpc and a velocity monopole by $5.4 \pm 3.4$ km/s/Mpc, whereas the field-to-field scatter in $H_0$ is 5.2 km/s/Mpc. Weighting the posteriors from each realisation equally gives $H_0 = 68.4 \pm 5.9$ km/s/Mpc, while weighting each by its Bayesian evidence gives $72.3 \pm 2.6$ km/s/Mpc. The latter value is set by a single particularly high-evidence realisation, making it sensitive to the finite sampling of the reconstruction posterior. This ladder therefore cannot yet arbitrate the Hubble tension. Extending the TRGB data beyond the present ~1000 km/s, together with improved reconstructions of the local Universe, would reduce the field-to-field scatter well below the 5.2 km/s/Mpc we find here.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
The two high-precision local measurements of the Hubble constant H0 both employ a Type Ia supernova (SN) rung: Supernovae and H0 for the Equation of State of dark energy (SH0ES) anchors on Cepheid–SN hosts (Riess et al. 2016, 2018, 2021, 2022; Breuval et al. 2024), and the Carnegie– Chicago Hubble Program (CCHP) on tip of the red giant branch (TRGB)–SN hosts (Beaton et al. 2016; Freedman et al. 2019, 2025a,b). Although the two agree at the ∼1.2 σ level, SH0ES sits in ∼5 σ tension with Planck cosmic microwave background (CMB) constraints under ΛCDM, whereas the CCHP sits in ∼1.6 σ tension with the same reference (Planck Collaboration et al. 2020b; Tristram et al. 2024; Freedman et al. 2025a,b). The SN rung itself carries standardisation, host-selection, covariance, dust, and absolute-magnitude calibration systematics that propagate

⋆richard.stiskalek@physics.ox.ac.uk

into the inferred H0 (e.g. Mandel et al. 2022; Efstathiou 2025; Wojtak & Hjorth 2025; Carreres et al. 2025), motivating local-ladder tests that do not use it.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
An alternative route is to infer H0 directly from galaxies with both SN-independent distances and measured redshifts, omitting the SN rung entirely (Hubble 1929; Willick & Batra 2001; Kenworthy et al. 2022). Exemplifying this approach, Stiskalek et al. (2026c) forward-model the apparent magnitudes of individual Cepheid stars and the redshifts of their host galaxies in a hierarchical Bayesian model, and describe the local peculiar-velocity field with the Manticore-Local reconstruction (McAlpine et al. 2025). They obtain H0 = 71.1 ± 1.4 km s−1 Mpc−1 (Stiskalek et al. 2026c,d). Other routes that drop the Type Ia rung replace it with surface-brightness fluctuations (Blakeslee et al. 2021; Cantiello & Blakeslee 2023; Jensen et al. 2025), Tully–Fisher catalogues (Schombert et al. 2020; Tully et al. 2023; Boubel et al. 2024), or Type II SNe (de Jaeger et al. 2022; Vogl et al.

2 R. Stiskalek et al.

2025). These routes yield H0 values typically in the range ∼73–76 km s−1 Mpc−1.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: Water masers stand apart from these routes, providing a geometric, calibration-independent H0 measurement that is not tied to any stellar standard candle (Lo 2005). The sub-parsec disc of NGC 4258 was resolved by Miyoshi et al. (1995) and its geometric distance measured by Herrnstein et al. (1999). The method was later extended to a multi-galaxy sample by the Megamaser Cosmology Project (e.g. Braatz et al. 2007; Reid et al. 2009; Pesce et al. 2020) and recently revisited by Stiskalek & Desmond (2026). Gravitational-wave standard sirens are similarly calibrationindependent, with the luminosity distance set by the waveform amplitude. The redshift is supplied by an electromagnetic counterpart (GW170817; Abbott et al. 2017) or probabilistically by a galaxy catalogue when the event has no such counterpart (dark sirens; e.g. Abbott et al. 2023).

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: The TRGB is the sharp cut-off at the bright end of the luminosity function of red giants, produced when their electron-degenerate helium cores ignite at a nearly fixed mass and therefore, at fixed composition, at a nearly fixed bolometric luminosity (Salaris & Cassisi 1997; Serenelli et al. 2017). Mould & Kristian (1986) first used the tip to measure a distance, and Da Costa & Armandroff (1990) calibrated the giant branch as a standard sequence, but the measurement was only automated by Lee et al. (1993), who located the tip with a Sobel edge-detection filter applied to the luminosity function. Madore & Freedman (1995) then simulated the conditions under which that measurement is unbiased, showing that it degrades at low photometric signal-to-noise and with crowding and contamination by populations other than red giants, and requires ≳100 stars within one magnitude of the tip. The TRGB is a Population II halo indicator with different dust, star-formation, and metallicity systematics from Cepheids (Anand et al. 2022; Bhardwaj et al. 2023; Li et al. 2024). In this work we construct a distance ladder from TRGB hosts and geometric anchors. The closest work in the literature is that of Kim et al. (2020), who infer H0 = 65.8 ± 3.5 (stat) ± 2.4 (sys) km s−1 Mpc−1 from TRGB distances and redshifts of 33 galaxies between the Local Group and Virgo, modelling their spherical infall towards Virgo. Their spherical infall treatment follows the velocity–distance relation of Peirani & de Freitas Pacheco (2006), who apply it separately to the Local Group and to Virgo. The same single-structure approach has since been extended to the Coma cluster (Benisty et al. 2026). Here we perform the direct TRGB analogue of the Cepheid-only analysis: an H0 inference from a TRGB catalogue and the

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
ructure approach has since been extended to the Coma cluster (Benisty et al. 2026). Here we perform the direct TRGB analogue of the Cepheid-only analysis: an H0 inference from a TRGB catalogue and the host redshifts alone.

The Extragalactic Distance Database (EDD) TRGB catalogue of Anand et al. (2021) is well suited to this exercise. It provides nearly 500 hosts, about an order of magnitude more than the SH0ES Cepheid-host sample. The sample is nevertheless local, with all hosts at CMB-frame recession velocities ≲2150 km s−1 and the bulk at ≲1000 km s−1. Peculiar velocities are then comparable to the cosmological signal and must be carefully modelled (Kaiser 1988; Hui & Greene 2006; Davis et al. 2011; Carrick et al. 2015; McAlpine et al. 2025; Stiskalek et al. 2026b). It is also assembled from heterogeneous Hubble Space Telescope (HST) programmes with no single well-defined selection function, which can be

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: a significant source of systematic uncertainty (Hinton et al. 2017; Desmond et al. 2026; Stiskalek et al. 2026c). A TRGBonly inference therefore tests a different combination of stellar calibration and sample selection from the Cepheid-only inference, over a smaller redshift range (≲1000 km s−1 versus 3300 km s−1). We forward-model the tip magnitudes, the host redshifts, and the catalogue selection, with the TRGB anchored to the geometric distances of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC; Pietrzyński et al. 2019) and NGC 4258 (Reid et al. 2019). In this regime the peculiar-velocity reconstruction is the dominant modelling systematic. We therefore use Manticore-Local (McAlpine et al. 2025), a field-level density and velocity reconstruction of the local Universe built with the Bayesian Origin Reconstruction from Galaxies (BORG) algorithm (Jasche & Wandelt 2013; Lavaux & Jasche 2016; Jasche & Lavaux 2019). The reconstruction is constrained by 2M++, an all-sky redshift compilation out to ∼200 h−1 Mpc (Lavaux & Hudson 2011). Field-level BORG reconstructions of this type were recently benchmarked as the most accurate of the available low-redshift velocityfield models (Stiskalek et al. 2026b). Manticore-Local itself attains the highest Bayesian evidence across independent peculiar-velocity catalogues (McAlpine et al. 2025). We find that the 5.2 km s−1 Mpc−1 scatter in H0 across the Manticore-Local realisations, rather than the TRGB calibration, limits the precision of this ladder.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
The structure of this paper is as follows. In Section 2 we describe the TRGB sample and the geometric anchors. In Section 3 we set out the hierarchical forward model and the velocity-reconstruction variants. In Section 4 we present the results. In Section 5 we interpret them, compare with previous work, and set out the caveats. In Section 6 we summarise our findings and conclude.

All logarithms are base-10 unless otherwise stated. We use N(x; µ, σ2) to denote a one-dimensional normal distribution with mean µ and variance σ2 evaluated at x; in higher dimensions µ is a vector and σ2 is replaced by a covariance matrix. A variable x drawn from this distribution is denoted x ←- N(µ, σ2). We follow the convention that h ≡H0/(100 km s−1 Mpc−1).

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
We use the TRGB catalogue of Anand et al. (2021), who provide measurements from HST colour–magnitude diagrams of 556 nearby galaxies, of which 489 have a tip measurement. Here and below, F606W and F814W denote the HST filter passbands used for the tip colours and magnitudes. The catalogue distances adopt the F814W colour-standardisation calibration of Rizzi et al. (2007) used in the EDD reductions (Anand et al. 2021, 2022). Our EDD retrieval, made on 2026 March 12, returns 487 entries, two fewer than the 489 tip measurements of Anand et al. (2021). The difference arises because the retrieval joins their catalogue to the Cosmicflows-4 (Tully et al. 2023) TRGB distance table and retains only hosts present in both. From these we remove NGC 4258 and its satellite NGC 4258-DF6, since NGC 4258 enters the model as a geometric anchor with the F814W tip magnitude of Jang et al. (2021). We further drop six galaxies without a finite F814W tip magnitude, one with-

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
The baseline inference applies a bright-end truncation mobs > 22.1 mag, removing 44 nearby objects with tip distances ≲2 Mpc and leaving 401 hosts. The CMB-frame redshifts of the removed objects are typically negative and hence completely dominated by the peculiar velocity. The removed objects are predominantly Local Group members, with more than half (26 of 44) belonging to the M31 subgroup. The Galactic-plane mask of the selection model (|b| ⩾ 10◦; Section 3.3.1) removes a further 7 hosts, so 394 hosts enter the likelihood. We treat the removal of the hosts lacking a colour-standardisation term or a tabulated redshift as a data-availability cut rather than as a selection effect requiring explicit modelling. The bright-end magnitude truncation and the Galactic-plane mask are instead modelled explicitly in the inference. The redshift-availability cut is not random in distance: the 33 hosts without a tabulated redshift are dwarf companions of the M81 and Centaurus A groups at 3– 10 Mpc. Whether a redshift has been measured depends on host luminosity rather than on the tip magnitude or colour at fixed distance, so the removal should not bias the absolute calibration M0. It does deplete the sample towards two nearby groups over that distance range, which the magnitude and angular selection terms do not describe. We do not test this aspect. We convert the catalogue redshift of each host to the CMB rest frame, zCMB, and take the host sky position from the catalogue. We use the individual host redshift throughout and do not substitute a group-averaged value.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
Figure 1a shows the retained hosts in the joint mobs– czCMB plane, with marginal distributions for both observables. Figure 1b shows the sky distribution of the same hosts in Galactic coordinates, coloured by czCMB, with the directions of Virgo, Fornax, Ursa Major, Centaurus A, and M31 marked. The hosts concentrate towards these nearby overdensities, reflecting the anisotropic large-scale structure of the local Universe.

We model the F814W tip absolute magnitude as a linear function of the tip colour c about the pivot c⋆, following the EDD colour standardisation of Rizzi et al. (2007),

MF814W = M0 + αc (c −c⋆) , (3)

where the zero-point M0 and pivot c⋆are inferred jointly with the other model parameters. We fix the colour– magnitude slope to αc = 0.2, the value adopted by Anand et al. (2022). Positive αc means that redder tips are fainter in F814W. Freeing αc leaves it poorly constrained in our inference, so we keep it fixed at the EDD value. We do not use the EDD-reported distance moduli within the inference. Instead, we forward-model the tip magnitudes and redshifts to infer the distances as latent variables. The catalogue does not report a redshift uncertainty. We adopt a baseline value of 20 km s−1, which is in any case subdominant to the expected peculiar-velocity scatter σv. The retained rows define the per-host observed quantities (mobs, em, cobs, ec, czCMB, ecz) entering the likelihood.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: We calibrate the TRGB with two geometric anchors: the LMC and NGC 4258. The LMC has distance modulus µLMC = 18.477 ± 0.026 mag from detached eclipsing-binary distances (Pietrzyński et al. 2019) and F814W tip magnitude mLMC = 14.456 ± 0.018 mag (Hoyt 2023). NGC 4258 has distance modulus µN4258 = 29.397 ± 0.032 mag from water-maser orbits (Reid et al. 2019) and F814W tip magnitude mN4258 = 25.347 ± 0.044 mag (Jang et al. 2021). We identify the published anchor tip magnitudes with our mobs of Eq. (1).

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: We construct a generative model in which the TRGB calibration, geometric anchor distances, host redshifts, and catalogue selection are all forward-modelled together. This requires a set of global parameters describing the population and a set of per-host latent variables. We summarise the model in a directed acyclic graph in Fig. 2, and tabulate all model parameters and their priors in Table A1 of Appendix A. We describe each component below.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
The inference requires external models of the density and velocity fields of the local Universe, for two reasons. First, most hosts lie at czCMB ≲1000 km s−1, where peculiar velocities of a few hundred km s−1 are a substantial fraction of the recession velocity. Second, the hosts trace the local large-scale structure through the galaxy bias rather than filling space uniformly, so the prior probability that a host lies at a given position depends on the matter density field

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
Manticore-Local takes as input the 2M++ galaxy compilation of Lavaux & Hudson (2011). The compilation comprises 69,160 galaxies from 2MASS (Skrutskie et al. 2006) with redshifts from 2MRS (Huchra et al. 2012), 6dF- GRS (Jones et al. 2009), and SDSS DR7 (Abazajian et al. 2009). It is Ks-limited at 11.5 in the 2MRS region and 12.5 elsewhere, with the usual photometric corrections applied. Manticore-Local is a field-level inference of the local Universe with the BORG algorithm (Jasche & Wandelt 2013; Lavaux & Jasche 2016; Jasche & Lavaux 2019). Linear initial conditions at z = 1000 are sampled by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on a 2563 grid in a 681 h−1 Mpc box, giving an inference resolution of 2.66 h−1 Mpc. The galaxybias model is specified per magnitude and redshift bin, with a generalised-Poisson likelihood. The initial conditions are evolved to z = 0, with COLA, a comoving Lagrangian acceleration solver, simulating the gravitational evolution from z = 69 onwards (Tassev et al. 2013; Stopyra et al. 2024). The inference adopts the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 “3×2pt + All Ext.” ΛCDM cosmology (Abbott et al. 2022), with h = 0.681 and Ωm = 0.306. Because the field coordinates in h−1 Mpc are set by the observed redshifts, we read the fields at h ri using the sampled H0 rather than the fixed h = 0.681.

In this work we use the 80 posterior realisations evolved to z = 0 with COLA at the native BORG settings. Their

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: density and velocity fields are deposited on a 2563 grid with the piecewise-cubic-spline mass-assignment scheme. In the baseline configuration we smooth the density field with a Gaussian kernel of width 4 h−1 Mpc and leave the peculiar-velocity field unsmoothed. The constrained volume extends to r ≲155 h−1 Mpc, set by the 2M++ completeness. McAlpine et al. (2025) validate the reconstruction with posterior predictive tests of the matter power spectrum, the bispectrum, the halo mass function, and the Gaussianity of the inferred initial conditions, and with the recovery of the local cluster catalogue. The velocity field is validated separately with the “Velocity Field Olympics” methodology (Stiskalek et al. 2026b). We condition the inference on one realisation at a time and combine the 80 resulting posteriors afterwards, under the two weightings defined in Section 3.4.

(2013) selects a galaxy if VLG < 600 km s−1 or D < 11 Mpc. Because either condition alone suffices, the parent list truncates neither czCMB nor mobs, so no selection term of either form follows from it. The magnitude window we adopt below stands as a posited proxy for the depth of the archival imaging. A secondary dependence is on host properties: the dominant HST programme targets unobscured, bright galaxies, and tip detectability depends further on star-formation history and crowding (Anand et al. 2021). None of these reduces to a simple mobs selection. We further restrict the observable sky with a Galactic-plane mask and allow an angular skyexposure extension (Section 3.3.1). Because the observed angular coordinate enters as a delta-function angular likelihood, the host term collapses onto the observed LOS, whereas the selection term remains an integral over the full survey volume. dr r2p(S = 1 | r, Λ). Since the Manticore-Local density field is defined on a regular grid, we evaluate the volume integral as a sum over V, a 75 Mpc sphere around the observer. This choice is sufficient because the p(S = 1 | r, Λ) term assigns negligible weight to any volume outside it. The selection integrand has support only to ∼10 Mpc, comparable to the 3.9 Mpc voxel size of the Manticore-Local fields, so a direct voxel sum would render the integral noisy. We therefore super-resolve every voxel within ∼20 Mpc by splitting it into 512 subcells of spacing ∼0.5 Mpc, evaluating the fields at the subcell centres by trilinear interpolation and dividing the parent volume weight among them. Because we model the selection as a function of magnitude, it is independent of the velocity field, Vext, and σv.

Two angular terms enter the selection model in addition to the magnitude window. First, we restrict to Galactic latitudes |b| ⩾bmin with bmin = 10◦, an approximate Zone-of- Avoidance mask reflecting the absence of TRGB data where extinction prevents their measurement (Kraan-Korteweg & Lahav 2000; Kraan-Korteweg 2005). The mask multiplies the integrand of Eq. (27) by an indicator function, so the population-detected fraction is evaluated over the unmasked volume only.

Second, in the variants labelled “sky exposure” we allow the detection probability to depend on direction as well, since the HST pointing history does not sample the sky uniformly. In these variants we partition the sky into Npix equalarea HEALPix pixels (Górski et al. 2005), indexed by q, and assign each a direction-dependent exposure weight θq. We test an Nside = 1 partition (Npix = 12) and a finer Nside = 2 partition (Npix = 48). The weight enters the selection in two places: it multiplies the magnitude term of Eq. (26) for a host

lying in the qth pixel, and it weights the corresponding contribution to the volume integral. The population-detected fraction of Eq. (27) then becomes the exposure-weighted sum S(k)(Λ) ∝P

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: We first present the baseline inference (Section 4.1) and test it against the data with posterior predictive checks (Section 4.1.1). We then quantify how the inference depends on each modelling choice in turn: the redshift likelihood (Section 4.2), the density-field smoothing scale (Section 4.3), the angular sky-exposure model (Section 4.4), and the flow modelling (Section 4.5). Throughout we quote each result under the two treatments of the Manticore-Local realisations defined in Section 3.4, the evidence-weighted and the equal-weight. We compare variants by the evidence as set out in Section 3.5. The results are tabulated in Table 1, which reports the two treatments side by side for each variant.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
We select the baseline variant by its ensemble evidence Zens. It is dominated by a single realisation, as we show below, so we check each ranking against the equally weighted ∆log Zfield. The two typically agree. The baseline model is the Manticore-Local reconstruction with 4 h−1 Mpc density smoothing, a Student-t redshift likelihood, and the 48-pixel angular sky-exposure selection term. The evidence-weighted constraint is H0 = 72.3 ± 2.6 km s−1 Mpc−1 (Table 1). Stacking the same per-field posteriors with equal weights instead gives H0 = 68.4 ± 5.9 km s−1 Mpc−1, and Fig. 3 shows the baseline H0 posterior under both treatments. The 80 field medians scatter about the equal-weight median with a standard deviation of 5.2 km s−1 Mpc−1 (Fig. 4). The 5.9 km s−1 Mpc−1 equal-weight width is essentially the quadrature sum of this scatter and the ∼2.6 km s−1 Mpc−1

mean single-field uncertainty. The field-to-field scatter therefore limits the equal-weight constraint, not the per-field statistical precision. The evidence shows no significant preference between this baseline and the velocity-monopole variant. That variant gives an H0 consistent with the baseline

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: The evidence-weighted posterior of Eq. (30) has Neff = 1.00 out of 80. The single-field evidences scatter by 6.7 in log Z, and the dominant realisation exceeds the runner-up by ∆log Z = 6.4. The four next-best realisations have field medians between 66.7 and 82.2 km s−1 Mpc−1. The physical reason is that the TRGB hosts mostly lie at czCMB ≲ 1000 km s−1 and each probes δ and V on the small scales that the 2M++ constraints determine least well. Hence the 80 Manticore-Local realisations, which agree on the largescale flow, still differ slightly in how well they explain these redshifts. Since the likelihood is a product over the 394 hosts, these small per-host differences compound, making the realisations meaningfully different. An ensemble of 80 is therefore too small to marginalise the field out, since the dominant realisation would likely differ for a different set of draws. The evidence-weighted stack is the marginal over the reconstruction posterior, and its limitation is that we approximate this marginal with only 80 samples. The equal-weight stack is not a marginalisation but is what follows if all 80 realisations are equally plausible, so the two together bracket the sensitivity to the reconstruction.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: The TRGB calibration and selection parameters remain unchanged across the model variants. The tip zeropoint is M0 = −4.03 ± 0.08 mag and the intrinsic scatter σint = 0.10 ± 0.01 mag, recovered within these uncertainties by all model variants. We note that we impose an informative prior on σint. It is obtained by inferring the TRGB distances from the tip magnitudes alone, calibrated on the same LMC and NGC 4258 geometric anchors as in the rest of this work, but without the density and velocity fields or redshift information and hence without inferring H0. The prior breaks the partial degeneracy between σint and the peculiarvelocity scatter σv. The σint posterior in the H0 inference then simply returns this prior, so the unchanging σint across the variants is in part imposed by this prior rather than being an independent confirmation of the stellar calibration. The selection edge falls within the observed magnitude range rather than beyond its faint end, so the incompleteness rolloff is sampled by the data: mlim = 24.07 ± 0.19 mag and σsel = 0.93±0.06 mag in the baseline run. The full posterior corner of the baseline run is shown in Fig. A1 and the additional nuisance-parameter posteriors for the main variants in Table A2, both in Appendix A. The mock validation of the pipeline is presented in Appendix B.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
Holding the density-field smoothing fixed at 4 h−1 Mpc, we test the sensitivity of the inference to the redshift likelihood choice. The evidence favours the Student-t over the Gaussian in every variant of Table 1. In the baseline configuration the preference is ∆log Zfield = +31.6 ± 4.4 and ∆log Zens = +36.2.

The two likelihood choices yield different H0 values under evidence weighting: the Gaussian Manticore-Local run gives H0 = 67.0 ± 2.6 km s−1 Mpc−1 and the Studentt run 72.3 ± 2.6 km s−1 Mpc−1. Equal-weight stacked, the two instead lie close together, at 69.4 ± 5.5 and 68.4 ± 5.9 km s−1 Mpc−1. The difference in the evidence-weighted H0 arises because the two likelihoods select different dominant realisations, which have different H0 medians. Field by field, the Student-t likelihood gives an H0 lower than the Gaussian by 0.8 ± 0.9 km s−1 Mpc−1. We therefore report both treatments throughout.

The inferred residual distribution is strongly non- Gaussian, with a tail index of ν = 2.59 ± 0.48. At this tail index the distribution is far from Gaussian, so the scale σv is no longer representative of a physical velocity dispersion. Figure 7 contrasts the two residual distributions at their inferred scales, σv ≃67 km s−1 under the Student-t against 132 km s−1 under the Gaussian. These heavy tails likely represent small-scale infall: many TRGB hosts cluster around

Virgo, Fornax, and Centaurus A, where the COLA reconstruction cannot resolve the virial motions.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
We now adopt the Student-t redshift likelihood and vary the density smoothing scale, retaining the 4 h−1 Mpc Student-t configuration as the reference. Under the equal-weight stack, doubling the density smoothing from 4 to 8 h−1 Mpc moves the Student-t inference from H0 = 68.4 ± 5.9 to 68.5 ± 5.8 km s−1 Mpc−1. Neither scale is significantly preferred, with the finer 4 h−1 Mpc leading 8 h−1 Mpc by ∆log Zfield = +1.9 ± 2.0 (Table 1). We verify that removing the density smoothing entirely leaves the equal-weight stacked Studentt H0 at 68.1 ± 6.0 km s−1 Mpc−1, consistent with the 4 and 8 h−1 Mpc values. The unsmoothed model is nevertheless disfavoured by ∆log Zfield = 6.2±5.9 relative to 4 h−1 Mpc.

Evidence-weighted, the 4 and 8 h−1 Mpc runs likewise agree, at H0 = 72.3 ± 2.6 and 72.4 ± 2.7 km s−1 Mpc−1, because the same realisation dominates both. Removing the smoothing instead moves the evidence-weighted value to 64.8±2.7 km s−1 Mpc−1 by changing which realisation dominates the mixture. At fixed realisation the smoothing scale has little effect: relative to 4 h−1 Mpc, the 8 h−1 Mpc run shifts H0 by +0.11±0.13 km s−1 Mpc−1 and the unsmoothed run by −0.26 ± 0.43 km s−1 Mpc−1.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
The angular sky-exposure selection term is decisively preferred, at ∆log Zfield = +44.4 ± 3.9 and ∆log Zens = +45.9 under the Student-t likelihood. It nevertheless leaves H0 unchanged under both treatments (Table 1).

The sky-exposure term is, however, required for the posterior predictive distributions to match the data, as shown in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6. At the dominant realisation the twosample KS p-value for the redshift distribution rises from 0.012 without it to 0.23 with it, whereas the magnitude pvalue stays near 0.07–0.11. We have verified that repeating the posterior predictive check over the 80 realisations leaves both the redshift and the magnitude p-values in the same range as at the highest-evidence realisation, so the qualitative outcome is unchanged. Inferring the 48 angular weights is a substitute for what should ideally be done: constructing the sky-exposure map from the actual HST pointing footprints of the EDD hosts, which the archival compilation does not record.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
We test both the 12-pixel (Nside = 1) and 48-pixel (Nside = 2) partitions of Section 3.3.1, and the baseline adopts the finer 48-pixel map. The evidence favours the 48pixel map over the 12-pixel one by ∆log Zfield ≃+19 under the Student-t likelihood, while the central value of H0 is unchanged (Table 1). We do not refine the partition further: the 48-pixel map already has only ∼8 of the 394 hosts per pixel on average. An Nside = 4 partition would leave ∼2, below the Dirichlet concentration α = 4 of Section 3.3.1, so the exposure weights would be prior-dominated. Field by field, the angular term barely moves the inference: at fixed realisation, adding the 48-pixel term to the no-exposure model shifts H0 by −0.02 ± 0.15 km s−1 Mpc−1, below 0.6 km s−1 Mpc−1 for every one of the 80 realisations. Refining from 12 to 48 pixels shifts it by +0.11 ± 0.10 km s−1 Mpc−1.

We now consider how the inferred H0 depends on modifications to the Manticore-Local velocity field. title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: We first discuss the local density and velocity field, which sets the limiting uncertainty of this measurement (Section 5.1), then the selection, galaxy-bias, and calibration systematics that are subdominant to it (Section 5.2), and finally the comparison with previous work (Section 5.3). Our central argument is that the precision of this two-rung ladder is set by the reconstruction of the local flow, and that the stellar and selection systematics become relevant only once that limit is lifted.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
section: The local density and velocity field
text: The limiting factor in this inference is not the TRGB calibration but our knowledge of the local density and velocity field that the TRGB hosts probe. The evidence-weighted H0 uncertainty is 2.6 km s−1 Mpc−1, whereas across the 80 Manticore-Local realisations the field-median H0 scatters by 5.2 km s−1 Mpc−1 in the baseline inference. That scatter is comparable to the difference between the SH0ES and Planck ΛCDM values that a local measurement is meant to arbitrate. The hosts lie at czCMB ≲2150 km s−1 and are concentrated far below that limit, with 87 per cent of them within 1000 km s−1 and half within 560 km s−1. While the constrained simulations suppress cosmic variance on the largest scales, such a small volume leaves H0 sensitive to structures at the limit of what Manticore-Local can reconstruct.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
section: The local density and velocity field
text:
The evidence-weighted H0 is determined by a single dominant Manticore-Local field (Section 4.1). The marginalisation is formally well motivated, but here its outcome is set by whichever realisation happens to dominate. The equal-weight stack is not an alternative marginalisation but a measure of the reconstruction-to-reconstruction uncertainty, so we quote the two side by side. Most of the variant-to-variant shifts in the evidence-weighted H0 follow from this. At fixed realisation the redshift likelihood, density smoothing, and sky-exposure choices each move H0 by less than 1 km s−1 Mpc−1, yet across those same variants the evidence-weighted value spans 63.5 to 72.4 km s−1 Mpc−1, because the dominant realisation changes between them. The velocity monopole is the sole exception: it raises H0 by 5.4 ± 3.4 km s−1 Mpc−1 at fixed realisation but by only 1.3 km s−1 Mpc−1 after evidence weighting. The evidence picks out the Manticore-Local Student-t class as the favoured model and strongly disfavours every Gaussianlikelihood variant relative to that baseline.

We take the density and velocity fields from Manticore-Local (McAlpine et al. 2025) and treat them as given. That makes the inference conditional on that set of posterior samples of the local Universe, on the 2M++ data and ΛCDM prior that constrain it, and on the other BORG modelling assumptions that generate it, mainly the reconstruction resolution, the galaxy-bias model, the count likelihood, and the particle-mesh gravity solver. The clearest sign that these assumptions leave the reconstructed flow incomplete is internal to the reconstruction: at the observer

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
section: The local density and velocity field
text:
position Manticore-Local predicts 368 ± 45 km s−1 where the Local-Group dipole requires 620 ± 15 km s−1, a deficit of ∼250 km s−1 that the “external” bulk flow has to model. Added to the reconstructed velocity at the observer, the equal-weight stacked Vext recovers the Planck Local-Group dipole in both amplitude and direction (Section 4.5).

Under the Gaussian likelihood we infer σv = 124 ± 5 km s−1 evidence-weighted and 132±7 km s−1 equal-weight stacked (Table 1). These sit 1.8σ and 1.5σ respectively from the 173 ± 27 km s−1 obtained for the extragalactic Cepheid hosts of Stiskalek et al. (2026c) under the same likelihood and the same Manticore-Local reconstruction. That redshift likelihood class is nonetheless the one the evidence rejects, by ∆log Zfield = 31.6 ± 4.4, so the physically meaningful residual is the one implied by the baseline Student-t. For a scale σv and tail index ν the implied root mean square is σv

p

ν/(ν −2), which for the equal-weight stacked (67 ± 7 km s−1, 2.59 ± 0.48) gives 141 km s−1, and for the evidence-weighted (57 ± 5 km s−1, 2.34 ± 0.34) gives 149 km s−1. The incompleteness of the reconstruction over this volume therefore shows up mainly in the coherent Vext, not in an inflated scatter relative to the Cepheid hosts.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
section: The local density and velocity field
text: This large Vext is not wholly unexpected, because the reconstructed flow at the observer position is colder than the CMB dipole would require (McAlpine et al. 2025). The reconstruction is constrained by the 2M++ redshift survey, whereas the dipole can be sourced in part by structure beyond that volume (Peacock 1992; Lavaux et al. 2010; Bilicki et al. 2011; Stiskalek et al. 2026a). We nevertheless adopt Manticore-Local over the linear-theory reconstruction of Carrick et al. (2015) and other literature fields (Lilow & Nusser 2021; Courtois et al. 2023) because it is favoured by the Bayesian evidence when evaluated against direct distance tracers (McAlpine et al. 2025; Stiskalek et al. 2026b). It also supplies an ensemble of posterior samples rather than a single point estimate, which is what lets us quantify the residual cosmic variance at all.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
section: The local density and velocity field
text:
Two data improvements would reduce this sensitivity to the flow model. The first is a TRGB sample extending well beyond the present limit, where the peculiar velocity is a few per cent of the recession velocity rather than the tens of per cent it reaches here. At those depths the residual sensitivity to non-linear peculiar velocities is small: relative to a 2M++-based reconstruction, ignoring them raises H0 by only ∼0.4±0.5 km s−1 Mpc−1 over 0.023 < z < 0.046 (Tsaprazi & Heavens 2025). The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has already measured a tip at 30 ± 4 Mpc (Carleton et al. 2024), and Anand et al. (2021) project TRGB distances out to 30–40 Mpc with modest exposure times, so the required depth is within reach. That first measurement is a favourable case rather than a typical host: a quiescent lowsurface-brightness dwarf with minimal crowding and 94 stars surviving the photometric cuts. The exposure required for a crowded disc at the same distance is therefore longer. What such programmes do not supply is a sample suited to a two-rung ladder: their targets are chosen because they host SNe Ia or have distances from surface-brightness fluctuations (Blakeslee et al. 2023; Li & Beaton 2024; Freedman et al. 2025a), so the selection is inherited mainly from the third rung rather than specified in terms of the tip observables.

The second is a constraint on the local initial conditions

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
section: The local density and velocity field
text: from data more local than the 2M++ redshift survey. Conditioning the reconstruction on such data would mean drawing realisations that explain the specific volume the TRGB hosts occupy, which would be expected to narrow the field-to-field spread. This would require extending the BORG framework to direct distance tracers, a step demonstrated on mock data by Prideaux-Ghee et al. (2023). Bayesian reconstruction from peculiar velocities alone has already been applied to real catalogues (Boruah et al. 2022). Alternative reconstructions of the local density and velocity field from direct distance tracers already exist (Courtois et al. 2023; Valade et al. 2022, 2026), but none of them targets the very local volume we consider here. There is nonetheless strong precedent for pushing BORG to even smaller scales: the positions and peculiar velocities of nearby galaxies have been used to constrain the Milky Way–Andromeda pair itself (Wempe et al. 2024, 2026). We do not use those reconstructions here because they do not explicitly model the Virgo Cluster, the dominant structure and source of infall within the TRGB volume.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
section: The local density and velocity field
text: A spatially constant radial inflow or outflow, the velocity monopole Vmono, is unphysical over a large volume and partly degenerate with H0 because a uniform radial flow mimics a change in the recession rate. The degeneracy is not perfect, because the recession velocity grows linearly with distance whereas Vmono, as we formulate it, does not, so a sample spanning a range of distances separates the two. Over the shallow TRGB volume the monopole is nonetheless a defensible first-order nuisance term, absorbing any residual monopole in the reconstruction itself. We therefore carry it as a variant rather than in the baseline. The inferred Vmono = −38.5 ± 27.2 km s−1 is consistent with zero, so the variant provides no evidence for a net radial flow within the TRGB volume. Constraining the local initial conditions jointly with the more local data discussed above would allow any residual monopole in the reconstruction to be modelled explicitly, rather than absorbed into a free nuisance term.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
When an archival compilation has no record of how its entries were assembled, its selection function can only be posited and partially constrained by the data in retrospect. This makes the inference conditional on a model that may be misspecified. We posit a selection on the tip apparent magnitude. Any additional selection would have to act on a different observable, most plausibly the redshift, or the magnitude selection itself would have to depart from the simple cumulative-normal form we assume.

We do not include a redshift-dependent selection term, even though velocity plays a part in how the parent sample was assembled: Karachentsev et al. (2013) include a galaxy if VLG < 600 km s−1 or D < 11 Mpc (Section 3.3). Because either condition alone suffices, a galaxy above the velocity threshold still enters the list on its distance. Redshift is in any case a poor distance indicator in this volume, since peculiar velocities of ∼300 km s−1 and Virgo infall of ∼180 km s−1

are comparable to the 600 km s−1 threshold itself. Since distance is also not an observable, we posit an effective selection on the apparent tip magnitude instead. The magnitude selection we posit reflects the depth of the imaging: Anand

et al. (2021) measure the tip out to just past 20 Mpc, a limit set by the exposure time needed to resolve the red giant branch rather than by a sharp failure of the method. The posterior predictive checks of Fig. 6 support a magnitudeonly selection, in that the magnitude-based model reproduces the observed redshift distribution of the hosts. No redshift-dependent selection is therefore required to explain the data, although the magnitude comparison itself remains marginal.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: A further question that neither the selection term nor that check probes is how the hosts trace the underlying density field. The dominant HST programme targets known unobscured galaxies within 10 Mpc, the range over which a single orbit resolves the red giant branch well enough for a tip measurement (Anand et al. 2021). We model this galaxy population with the inhomogeneous-Malmquist prior, whose bias term we can only posit. We verify that the equalweight stacked H0 moves by less than 1 km s−1 Mpc−1 across the variants that shift the inferred bias slope from αlow = 2.25 ± 0.39 to 4.26 ± 0.59 (Tables 1 and A2), so this dependence is subdominant to the field-to-field scatter. We infer the limiting magnitude to be mlim = 24.07 ± 0.19 mag with a smooth transition width σsel = 0.93 ± 0.06 mag. The evidence prefers the angular sky-exposure term at ∆log Zfield = +44.4 ± 3.9, plausibly because the archival campaigns targeted rich regions of the sky rather than sampling the volume uniformly. Surveys that fix their filters, depth, and sky coverage in advance would ideally make these parameters known rather than inferred. The proposed Roman wide-area programme would do so (Blakeslee et al. 2023), its selection well specified even though its targets are inherited from the surface-brightness-fluctuation and SN rungs, as would ground-based resolved-star searches whose completeness is calibrated against image simulations (Mutlu-Pakdil et al. 2021). A further astrophysical uncertainty is the assumed galaxy-bias model, which maps the Manticore-Local matter field to the expected host number density entering the inhomogeneous-Malmquist term. This mapping is required in any full physical forward model, but is poorly constrained. At the level of dark matter haloes the bias is a power law

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
er density entering the inhomogeneous-Malmquist term. This mapping is required in any full physical forward model, but is poorly constrained. At the level of dark matter haloes the bias is a power law in the local density with an exponential downturn that suppresses occupation in voids (Neyrinck et al. 2014). Manticore-Local generalises this to a sigmoid-truncated double power law, adding a second slope at high density and replacing the exponential cutoff with a sigmoid (McAlpine et al. 2025). The form we adopt in Eq. (6), here and in our previous Cepheid-only analysis (Stiskalek et al. 2026c), retains the two power-law regimes but not the low-density truncation. Bartlett et al. (2024) show, however, that localin-density bias models do not reproduce the clustering of the halo field on the smoothing scales and at the halo masses relevant to our 4 h−1 Mpc field. Moreover, the TRGB hosts are predominantly nearby low-mass galaxies, a regime in which the bias prescriptions we adopt have never been calibrated. Neyrinck et al. (2014), for example, characterise the bias of dark matter haloes rather than of the galaxies occupying them. The mapping we require is therefore harder than the halo case that already fails, since it must additionally describe the occupation of low-mass galaxies within those haloes.

This matters most for a sample as nearby as ours, whose

MNRAS 000, 1–21 (2026)

16 R. Stiskalek et al.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
distance uncertainties localise individual hosts within specific structures, so the bias model acts on resolved features of the density field rather than on a smooth average. As a related example, when comparing the second data release of the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF DR2) Type Ia SNe with the same Manticore-Local reconstruction, Gilles Lordet et al. (2026) find that the SN rate is not a linear tracer of the matter density, reaching local enhancements of a factor of two to five within nearby clusters. Table A2 and Fig. A1 give the posteriors of b across the variants.

The TRGB calibration contributes two further systematics. The tip is standardised at a fixed colour pivot with the slope held at αc = 0.2 (Anand et al. 2022), so any residual colour or metallicity dependence propagates into M0. The EDD compilation also aggregates measurements from heterogeneous HST programmes, where a different edgedetection algorithm can shift the inferred tip (Scolnic et al. 2023). The two enter the inference differently. The colourpivot systematic acts coherently across the sample, so it enters as a single offset in M0 and hence a single offset in H0. The algorithmic heterogeneity instead varies between programmes and enters as additional scatter in the individual tip magnitudes. Neither systematic can generate the 5.2 km s−1 Mpc−1 field-to-field spread in H0, because the same tip magnitudes enter the inference for every field. A coherent offset ∆M0 shifts H0 by approximately the same fraction, ≈0.46 ∆M0, in every field, so it moves the headline value but not the spread between fields. The programme-toprogramme scatter is absorbed by σint, whose prior is inferred from the same heterogeneous tip magnitudes and so already includes it.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
Our constraint is consistent with the published TRGB ladders that retain the SN third rung, but is less precise than the CCHP and CATS values by a factor of ∼1.2–1.4 under the evidence-weighted treatment and ∼3 under the equal-weight one. The consistency therefore follows in large part from that lower precision. The CCHP infers H0 = 70.4±1.2 (stat)±1.3 (sys)±0.7 (σSN) km s−1 Mpc−1 (Freedman et al. 2025a,b), the CATS reanalysis gives 73.2 ± 2.1 km s−1 Mpc−1 (Scolnic et al. 2023), and a ladder built exclusively from SNe Ia in quiescent, early-type hosts gives 75.3 ± 2.9 km s−1 Mpc−1 (Newman et al. 2026). That calibrator sample is deliberately disjoint from the starforming hosts on which Cepheid calibrations rely. Scolnic et al. (2023) decompose the 3.4 km s−1 Mpc−1 separating their value from the earlier CCHP result of 69.8 ± 1.9 km s−1 Mpc−1 (Freedman et al. 2019) into 2.0 km s−1 Mpc−1 from SN-survey and peculiar-flow corrections absent in that work and 1.4 km s−1 Mpc−1 from the inhomogeneity of the TRGB calibration across the ladder. Freedman & Madore (2023) challenge two of the tip identifications that enter that reanalysis. For NGC 4038 and NGC 4536, the tip measurements that CATS weights most highly give distance moduli 0.7 and 0.6 mag smaller, respectively, than the SH0ES Cepheid moduli for the same hosts. The offsets are attributed to the unsupervised edge detection selecting the tip of the asymptotic giant branch rather than the TRGB, with NGC 4038 as the explicit example. Those analyses use the TRGB only to calibrate a second

rung reaching cz ≳3000 km s−1, where peculiar velocities are a few per cent of the recession velocity.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: The TRGB-only measurements that precede ours confront the same flow dependence, but address it by modelling infall onto a single structure. Kim et al. (2020) obtain 65.8±3.5 (stat)±2.4 (sys) km s−1 Mpc−1 from galaxies falling towards Virgo, solving a spherical infall model that includes ΩΛ and inferring H0 jointly with the Virgo turnaround radius R0 = 6.76 ± 0.35 Mpc and a residual velocity scatter σv = 62 ± 14 km s−1. The same infall approach was applied separately to the Local Group and to Virgo by Peirani & de Freitas Pacheco (2006), and later extended to Coma with distances other than the TRGB (Benisty et al. 2026). We instead predict the flow at every host position from the reconstructed field, which replaces a single-structure infall model with a more complete description of the local density and velocity field.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
Both high-precision local anchors of the Hubble tension rely on the Type Ia SN rung (Riess et al. 2022; Freedman et al. 2025a). In this paper we have tested how well the local ladder constrains H0 without that rung, using only the TRGB stellar indicator and the host redshifts and geometric anchors, following the Cepheid-only precedent of Stiskalek et al. (2026c). We have forward-modelled the tip magnitudes and their latent colours (standardised at the fixed slope αc = 0.2), the host redshifts, the magnitude-limited catalogue selection with its Galactic-plane mask and angular sky-exposure variants, and the LMC and NGC 4258 geometric anchors. We conditioned the inference on each of the 80 Manticore-Local realisations of the local density and peculiar-velocity fields in turn. We then stacked the resulting posteriors, weighted either equally or by their Bayesian evidence. Our main findings are as follows.

(i) The limiting uncertainty is the local density and especially velocity field, rather than the TRGB calibration. The field-median H0 scatters by 5.2 km s−1 Mpc−1 across the 80 Manticore-Local realisations, comparable to the SH0ES– Planck-ΛCDM difference.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text:
(ii) The equal-weight stack of the 80 single-field posteriors gives H0 = 68.4 ± 5.9 km s−1 Mpc−1, whereas weighting the same posteriors by their evidence gives 72.3 ± 2.6 km s−1 Mpc−1 in the baseline inference. The baseline adopts a Student-t redshift likelihood and is the highestevidence variant tested. Interpreting the per-field evidences as relative model probabilities gives an effective sample size of Neff = 1.00 out of 80, so this constraint has collapsed onto a single Manticore-Local realisation. The equal-weight stack is more conservative and follows from treating all realisations as equally plausible. The evidence-weighted value effectively assumes the single highest-evidence realisation to be true, which is likely sensitive to the particular sampling of the Manticore-Local BORG inference.

(iii) At fixed realisation the redshift likelihood, density smoothing, and sky-exposure choices each move H0 by less than 1 km s−1 Mpc−1. Only the addition of a velocity monopole moves it appreciably, raising H0 by 5.4 ± 3.4 km s−1 Mpc−1 at fixed realisation.

H0 from TRGB alone 17

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: This supernova-free distance ladder therefore does not yet deliver a precise H0. Across the variants of the velocity model, the equal-weight stacked H0 ranges from 68.4 ± 5.9 to 74.7 ± 5.2 km s−1 Mpc−1, so a TRGB-only ladder does not have the constraining power to distinguish the Planck and SH0ES values. The main limitation is the small volume the TRGB hosts probe. The density field enters through the inhomogeneous-Malmquist distance prior, whereas the velocity at the host positions maps directly into H0 through the redshift residuals. A TRGB-only ladder is far more sensitive to this than the geometry and Cepheid ladder of Stiskalek et al. (2026c) because 87 per cent of the TRGB hosts lie at czCMB < 1000 km s−1, where the flow is a large fraction of the recession velocity. This limitation is therefore not intrinsic to a two-rung ladder. Our Cepheidonly analysis uses the SH0ES Cepheid hosts, which reach 3300 km s−1 (Riess et al. 2022). There the same framework and the same Manticore-Local reconstruction give H0 = 71.1±1.4 km s−1 Mpc−1, with much weaker sensitivity to the density- and velocity-field treatment (Stiskalek et al. 2026c,d). The archival nature of the sample is a further limitation: the EDD compilation has no clear record of how its entries were assembled, so the magnitude and angular selection terms must be posited and inferred rather than specified a priori. The same is true of our Cepheid analysis (Stiskalek et al. 2026c,d). In the TRGB-only ladder the uncertainty from this unspecified selection is likely subdominant to the residual cosmic variance of the local flow. It nevertheless motivates recording the selection of future TRGB samples, so that the selection function can be specified rather than inferred.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone
text: More constructively, the collapse of the evidenceweighted posterior onto a single realisation shows how sensitive this inference is to the assumed model of the local Universe. The remaining gains are therefore in the modelling of the local Universe itself, in the density field that enters the inhomogeneous-Malmquist distance prior and especially in the velocity field that maps into the redshift residuals. At these distances H0 cannot be inferred without modelling the peculiar velocity of every host. Narrowing the field-to-field spread requires reconstructions constrained by data within the volume the hosts occupy, or a TRGB sample deep enough that the peculiar velocity is a smaller fraction of the recession velocity so that existing reconstructions such as Manticore-Local are sufficient. This matters beyond the present measurement, because the local volume anchors the calibration of the SNe: how it is modelled propagates into every H0 inferred through that rung.

title: Two-rung ladder: $H_0$ from Tip of the Red Giant Branch and geometric anchors alone

title: CHASE Spectral Survey I: Measuring Contamination in the Color-selected J-region Asymptotic Giant Branch Distance Indicator
text: The J-region asymptotic giant branch (JAGB) method for distance measurements uses the near uniform luminosity of carbon-rich AGB stars as a standard candle. Its application rests on an assumed but rarely examined premise: the stars contained in the JAGB color-magnitude selection box are primarily carbon-rich AGB stars. We investigate the purity of the photometric selection in the Milky Way with an optical spectroscopic survey (~3590-7150 $\mathring{A}$) called CHASE (Carbon stars, Hubble tension, And Spectroscopic Exploration of JAGB populations) using the Shane 3 m telescope at Lick Observatory. These stars are classified using molecular bandhead step indices, which recover 100% of known classifications. We report the observations of 76 stars (54 within the standard JAGB selection box of 1.5 < J - K < 2.0 mag) and find only 13 of 54 stars are carbon-rich, a 76$\pm$6 oxygen-rich contamination under blind photometric selection. This contamination remains high (71%) even within $\pm$0.4 mag of the JAGB peak itself, showing it is not confined to the edges of the selection box. This inhomogeneity may explain why recent literature find field-to-field and methodological variations of 0.1-0.2 mag that now dominate its systematic error budget. These variations could be caused, in part, by inhomogeneous stellar populations that consist of differing spectral types, and hence differing mean magnitudes.

title: CHASE Spectral Survey I: Measuring Contamination in the Color-selected J-region Asymptotic Giant Branch Distance Indicator
text:
The J-region asymptotic giant branch (JAGB) method for distance measurements uses the near uniform luminosity of carbon-rich AGB stars as a standard candle. Its application rests on an assumed but rarely examined premise: the stars contained in the JAGB color–magnitude selection box are primarily carbon-rich AGB stars. We investigate the purity of the photometric selection in the Milky Way with an optical spectroscopic survey (∼3590–7150 ˚A) called CHASE (Carbon stars, Hubble tension, And Spectroscopic Exploration of JAGB populations) using the Shane 3 m telescope at Lick Observatory. These stars are classified using molecular bandhead step indices, which recover 100% of known classifications. We report the observations of 76 stars (54 within the standard JAGB selection box of 1.5 < (J −Ks)0 < 2.0 mag) and find only 13 of 54 stars are carbon-rich, a 76 ± 6% oxygen-rich contamination under blind photometric selection. This contamination remains high (71%) even within ±0.4 mag of the JAGB peak itself, showing it is not confined to the edges of the selection box. This inhomogeneity may explain why recent literature find field-to-field and methodological variations of 0.1–0.2 mag that now dominate its systematic error budget. These variations could be caused, in part, by inhomogeneous stellar populations that consist of differing spectral types, and hence differing mean magnitudes.
