title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
In our baseline analysis, we employ ΛCDM with a free neutrino mass sum as the reference model for comparison. The models in section II extend it with the additional parameters described in that section. Their performance according to our various metrics is reported in tables II to VI, and summarized in figs. 1 and 2. Models that satisfy the threshold criteria of section III C are highlighted in red. Figure 3 shows the posteriors for the parameters (H0, Ωm, S8) in each model.

Overall, the rankings are relatively consistent across the various metrics.

1. Group E shows the best overall performance, reducing the tension to around the 3σ level while achieving ∆AIC values of order 20 or larger. The log-Bayes factor is also typically above 5, corresponding to decisive evidence, except for the cold NEDE model, for which it is around 3, corresponding to strong evidence. Within this group, the axion EDE model performs best according to Frequentist metrics, with −∆AIC = 23.4 and ∆DMAP = 2.5σ, and reaches the largest Bayes factor in the competition, ln BF ≃10.5. However, it is slightly outperformed in the Bayesian tension metrics by the cold NEDE model, for which ∆shift and ∆Gauss are both around 2.8σ.

2. Group M shows intermediate performance. The varying-electron-mass model reaches a residual tension of around 4σ, with −∆AIC = 12.6 and a log-Bayes factor of about 3.5, corresponding to very strong evidence. The 4-parameter modified recombination model achieves a good fit improvement, with −∆AIC = 9.8, but does not substantially reduce the tension metrics ∆shift, ∆Gauss, or ∆DMAP, which remain above 5σ, similarly to ΛCDM. Its log-Bayes factor is also close to zero, indicating no meaningful Bayesian preference over ΛCDM.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
3. Group R performs only marginally better than ΛCDM. The most successful model in this group is WZDR, which reduces the tension to roughly 4.5σ and reaches −∆AIC ≃8, with a log-Bayes factor of about 1.8, corresponding to substantial evidence. The other group R models perform worse, with negative log-Bayes factors and residual tensions around 5σ.

22

4. Groups L and E+L perform worst overall. These models generally do not significantly reduce the H0 tension and do not achieve competitive AIC improvements. The best-performing model in this group is the sign-switching cosmological constant model, which reaches a modest improvement, ∆AIC ≃−3.6, and a log-Bayes factor of about 0.92, corresponding to anecdotal evidence. However, the residual tension remains above 5σ for this model, as for the other contenders in groups L and E+L.

The weaker performance of group M, group E+L, and especially group R compared to previous literature [13, 145] can be attributed to the inclusion of ACT data, which prefer a higher amplitude of the angular power spectrum in the CMB damping tail, c.f. Ref. [2, Figs. 41,42] and Ref. [18, Fig. 3]. We discuss this point further in section IV E, where we check how these results shift if ACT data are removed.

Neutrino mass constraints. We show the neutrino mass constraints for all models in figs. 5 and 6. These Bayesian constraints depend on our choice of prior, P mν > 0. We investigate the consequences of priors motivated by neutrino oscillation experiments in section V D. The 95% credible interval for our data combination in ΛCDM is 0 < P mν < 66meV. This is mostly compatible with close-to-minimal normal hierarchy scenarios. The upper bound is not significantly different for other models, except for two cases:

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
1. In the case where the SROLL2 EE likelihood is dropped in ΛCDM (see section II L), the neutrino mass constraints relax significantly to P mν < 120meV (95% CL). This follows from the well-known degeneracy between the summed neutrino mass and the reionization optical depth τreio [172, 173, 203–205]. In absence of a low-ℓpolarization likelihood, the optical depth is poorly constrained and simultaneous high values of (P mν, τreio) are compatible with the data.

2. In the case where the electron mass varies between the early and late universe, the angular diameter distance to the last-scattering surface is free to change without impacting the CMB anisotropies at first order, as argued in Refs. [113, 119]. This generates a much stronger geometric degeneracy H0-P mν that can only be broken by late-time data. The model features a parameter degeneracy in which H0, P mν and mearly

e /mlate

e are all increased without impacting CMB angular power spectra significantly. As a result, the neutrino mass bounds weaken to P mν < 123meV (95% CL) and is dominated by BAO data – without BAO data it relaxes to P mν < 291meV (95% CL), which is the weakest bound of all tested combinations of data and models in this work.

For all other models, the neutrino mass bounds may weaken significantly (> 50%) only in combination with free curvature or dynamical dark energy parameters, see sections IV C and IV D. The neutrino mass constraints for each model can be found in section B, tables XII to XIV.

Other parameter constraints. All credible intervals are reported in section B, with table XI showing the parameters specific to each model and tables XII to XIV those common to all of them. For the constraints with a prior on MB added, see fig. 25 in section A.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
Impact of BAO and SNeIa. These results can also be compared to the corresponding analyses without supernovae or BAO data (that is, CMB-only or CMB+BAO), shown in section A, figs. 23 and 24. The main conclusion from these comparisons is that BAO data have the strongest impact on constraints for all model classes, while supernova data often play a subdominant role. Without BAO, models in groups R, M, and E are compatible with broader Ωm ranges, especially towards higher values, and neutrino mass bounds are significantly looser. This opening of the Ωm parameter space is strongly limited once BAO data are included.

Note that models relieving the Hubble tension usually feature a negative correlation between H0 and Ωm [124, 206, 207]. Thus, the fact that DESI BAO data favors smaller values of Ωm tends to help model in reducing the Hubble tension, as already found in [18, 89, 208–210].

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
Notable differences with previous literature. In the 4-parameter recombination model, our results with CMB+BAO+SN data are much more constraining than in previous analyses like Ref. [127]. We find a residual tension with SH0ES typically above 5σ. We checked that with the same data combination as in Ref. [127], which does not include ACT and SPT data, we get nearly the same result, H0 = (71.23±0.68)km/s/Mpc, as Ref. [127], H0 = (71.34±0.68)km/s/Mpc. Thus, the ability to reduce the tension is compromised by the addition of ACT and SPT data. Noticeable is the strong reduction in χ2 with CMB+BAO+SN data by ∆χ2 ≃−11, suggesting that the model is highly efficient at fitting the data, but penalized by its many parameters as well as its lack of preference for increased H0 values. It is important to stress that a truly flexible recombination model might still show better performance, but checking this is beyond the scope of this work.

The sign-switching ΛsCDM model also does not show such a strong performance in reducing the tension as in the previous literature. The reason is both the improved constraining power of the CMB data and the tighter BAO+SNeIa data. We note that our results are nevertheless very similar to [163, Tab III] or [162, Tab II]. The performance reported in some papers is enhanced by their use of transversal BAO data from SDSS. However, these data may suffer from radial mode leakage [211, 212] or redshift bin smearing for tophat bins [213]. Additionally, they do not capture the full constraining power of DESI BAO. We therefore do not consider transversal BAO data from SDSS here.

The thawing gravity model has been shown in Ref. [111] to be able to reduce the Hubble tension in the scaling regime for |ξ| < 3/16 for small values of |ξσ2

Instead, the data prefers a parameter space in which the thawing gravity model exhibits phantom crossing at low redshift for the effective dark energy parameter of state [106] for all the datasets considered, which is a distinctive signature of the attractor general relativity regime for |ξ| > 3/16. C. Baseline in a universe with evolving dark energy

The cosmological constant provides the simplest description of late-time acceleration, but current low-redshift data also motivate tests of more general dark-energy dynamics. In particular, recent DESI BAO [17, 196, 214, 215] and full-shape [216–218] data combined with CMB and SN measurements favor departures from ΛCDM in the CPL parametrization, with a preference at the 3–4σ level for an evolving equation of state that crosses into the phantom regime [219]. We find that for the considered CMB dataset, this preference is typically reduced to slightly above 2σ for the vanilla model – i.e. the model that reduces to ΛCDM in the limit (w0, wa) →(−1, 0), see table VII. The constraints in the w0, wa parameter space for all models are shown in fig. 7, while the full contours can be found in section C. The only model for which this preference is significantly reduced is the the Agnos. Reion. case of section II L, in which only a 1.2σ residual preference remains. Such a reduction is expected from the results of Ref. [173], which we confirm with up-to-date data.

For the Varying me model the preference is reduced from 2.3σ to 1.2σ (−1.1σ), whereas for the WZDR model it is reduced from 2.2σ to 1.5σ (−0.7σ), see table VII. The reason that forcing a reduction of the Hubble tension coincides with a reduction for preference of dynamical dark energy in these models is that they more strongly reduce Ωm when increasing H0 compared to other solutions – noting that the discrepancy of the Ωm value between BAO and CMB data appears to be partially driving the preference for dynamical dark energy. The constraints for these two models (together with the Agnos. Reion. model) are highlighted in fig. 8.

Finally, none of the models benefit from the inclusion of an evolving dark energy equation of state in their ability to ease the Hubble tension. For all models the tension metrics increase by up to 0.5σ – the only exclusion from this rule is the DRMD model for which tension metrics remain about the same (see tables II and III). For all models, the comparison metrics (∆AIC and Bayes Factor) worsen when dynamical dark energy is considered since the marginal improvement in overall fit is outweighed by the cost of the two additional parameters, see tables V and VI.

In summary, while the reduction of Ωm seen in most models that ease the Hubble tension is lowering the preference for dynamical dark energy observed in the DESI BAO data (especially when combined with SNeIa data), the allowance for dynamical dark energy does not help in mitigating the Hubble tension since the latter tends to lead to a decrease in the late time expansion rate.

D. Baseline in a curved universe

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
Another well motivated late-time extension of ΛCDM is spatial curvature, parametrized by Ωk . Similarly to dynamical dark energy, it was recently found to provide a better fit to CMB+DESI data [220]. It is also known that models affecting recombination such as the varying electron-mass model further reduce the Hubble tension if curvature is nonzero [13, 113, 119, 124]. Indeed, the best-performing model in Ref. [13] was the combination of varying me and nonzero curvature, which although phenomenologically well-understood [13, 113, 119, 124], lacks a deeper theoretical motivation as to why electron mass variations should be connected to curvature. Here, we follow a

This comparison is shown in fig. 9, where we display the constraints on the parameters most directly relevant to the Hubble tension, with and without curvature. Overall, we find that the impact of curvature is minor; see also tables II to VI.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
As found in Ref. [13], the largest effect is still obtained for the varying electron mass model. Allowing curvature increases the −∆AIC from 12.6 to 14.5, lowers ∆DMAP from 4.3σ to 3.5σ, and increases the log-Bayes factor from 3.5 (very strong evidence) to 4.9 (decisive evidence). The other Bayesian tension metrics are essentially unchanged. In the present analysis, the combined CMB dataset constrains curvature much more tightly, Ωk = (1.5 ± 1.6) × 10−3, compared to (−3.2 ± 5.0) × 10−3 in Ref. [13]. As a result, it provides less freedom to improve the varyingelectron-mass fit than it did in the previous analysis.

The other model that benefits substantially from nonzero curvature is the RnR model, for which the inclusion of curvature reduces the tension by about −0.4σ to −0.7σ depending on the metric, while increasing the log-Bayes factor from 7.7 to 10.8. This appears to be due to larger values of σini (which is most strongly correlated with H0 in this model) being more compatible with the CMB data when slightly larger Ωm values are considered – in this case the effect on late time observables can be compensated by a larger neutrino mass sum P mν together with positive curvature Ωk > 0. This can be checked in fig. 26.

E. No ACT runs

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
In this competition, many models are subject to significantly tighter constraints than what one would expect by plain extrapolation of increased uncertainty based on previous analyses like Ref. [13] that relied solely on Planck CMB data without taking into account the different multipole scales accessed.9 In most cases, the reason for this discrepancy is the interplay between ACT and Planck data leading to extremely strong constraints on deviations from ΛCDM, especially towards DR. The level of consistency of the ACT and Planck+SPT data has been a matter of debate, given the 2 −3σ tension between the value of Neff inferred from these CMB datasets [3, 7]. It is therefore instructive to assess the impact of ACT on the constraints and test their robustness when ACT data are excluded. We run analyses for the CMB+BAO+SN combination without any ACT data (lensing and primary CMB), while keeping the truncated Planck ℓ-range. In this case we find much more permissive constraints, as shown in figs. 10 and 11 as well as in tables VIIIa and VIIIb.

We observe that group R is benefiting the most from the removal of ACT data, followed by group M, with the other groups showing relatively stable results. The metrics for group R decrease from around 5σ with ACT data to 3 −3.5σ without it – the biggest improvement being for the DRMD model. In group M, the tension also improves from roughly 4σ to 3.6σ for the varying electron mass model. This confirms that ACT data are preventing several models from efficiently reducing the tension, especially when they involve DR.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
The tension metrics ∆shift and ∆Gauss remain roughly at the 5.5σ level for ΛCDM and models of groups L and E+L, whereas the Bayes factor improves quite a bit for the thawing gravity model. While the significantly lower mean value of H0 for thawing gravity prevents it from strongly reducing the tension in this case, it does generate a good fit over a wide range of H0 values, reflecting in the large uncertainty and higher Bayes factor.

A dedicated analysis is needed to pin down the reason of the large impact of ACT data on models of groups R and M. We note that ACT has a slight preference for higher power at high ℓ, c.f. Ref. [2, Figs. 41,42] and Ref. [18, Fig. 3]. We therefore surmise that its impact can be understood from the impact of each model on the high-ℓtail of the CMB power spectra (see in particular Ref. [153]). It is well known that models with enhanced radiation lead to a decrease of power on small scales [137, 153, 222], while EDE instead shows a strong upward curvature towards large ℓ[92, 123, 223]. The varying electron mass model “sits in between”, leaving the high-ℓtail similar to ΛCDM [113, 119, 123] The larger high-ℓtail in ACT data is therefore more beneficial for group E models than for group R and group M.

As shown in Ref. [224] a simple way to alter the high-ℓspectra and affect ACT constraints is to change the shape of the primordial power spectrum. We further discuss the impact of running and running of running on the other models in section IV F below. 10

F. Running of the primordial power spectrum

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
Most inflationary models predict a deviation from a primordial power spectrum PR(k) described by a simple power-law, which is the result of the simple single-field paradigm to lowest order in a slow-roll expansion. Higher orders in the slow-roll expansion naturally lead to a running of the spectral index (αs), or a running of the running of this index (βs) [225].

9 A notable exception is early dark energy models, for which the tension has decreased compared to pre-ACT and pre-DESI data, when it was at the 3.5σ level [96, 221]. 10 Another possibility suggested in the literature to weaken constraints on model with extra radiation is to exploit the “mirror world” symmetry of CMB observables [29–32]. We leave investigating this possibility for future work.

In typical slow-roll inflation, higher-order terms are expected to be suppressed by additional powers of the small slow-roll parameters, leading to a natural hierarchy βs ≪αs ≪ns −1 [226], such that these additional corrections would be negligible. However, if slow roll inflation is driven by multiple fields (see e.g. [227]) or if there are deviations from the slow-roll conditions (see e.g. [228, 229]), the higher order terms can become relevant. We truncate the series at third order and check if the data prefers significant deviations from the traditional slow roll limit, which we approximate as the point at which αs = βs = 0.

More general power spectrum modifications have been shown to lead to an increase in the inferred value of H0 from CMB data [230–233], often involving oscillatory modifications of the primordial power spectrum. We leave analyses with such oscillatory features in the primordial power spectrum to future work.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
This beyond slow-roll analysis is especially interesting in relation to the aforementioned preference for more power on small scales in the ACT data. For example, in the ΛCDM+αs+βs model the CMB+BAO+SN data combination yields αs = 0.0122 ± 0.0057 and βs = 0.0144 ± 0.088, clearly indicating a preference for an upturn at large k, corresponding to large ℓ. In fact, it has been found that in the SIDR and DRMD models the combination of Planck+ACT data favor non-zero αs and βs, while allowing for significantly larger H0 [224]. Here, we obtain similar results, αs = 0.0198 ±0.0081, βs = 0.022 ±0.010, and H0 = (69.40±0.74)km/s/Mpc where Ref. [224] with

36

only Planck+ACT data finds αs = 0.024±0.0082, βs = 0.0264+0.012

−0.061 and H0 = 69.94+0.84

−1.1 , suggesting that SPT data does not significantly alter these conclusions apart from slightly improving the constraint on the deviation from ΛCDM and the corresponding ability to ease the Hubble tension.

A preference for deviation from the slow-roll expectation (αs ≈0, βs ≈0) is also seen for other models, as shown in figs. 12 and 13, including for ΛCDM+αs + βs . As visible in fig. 12, models of group R favor even larger values of αs and βs than in the ΛCDM+αs+βs case. The varying me also shows a similar (albeit smaller) preference. In contrast, models in groups E and L yield results that are more compatible with a simple power-law than the ΛCDM+αs+βs case when a prior on MB is imposed. The 4param. Mod. Rec. case has entirely different contours in this case, both with and without a prior on MB, remaining roughly compatible with αs = 0 and preferring only slightly positive values of βs.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
Correspondingly, as visible in fig. 13, models of group R especially benefit from the expansion through αs and βs, in good agreement with Ref. [224]. In particular, fig. 13 highlights that the strong reduction in tension (up to the 3.5σ level) for group R reported in table IXb is only compatible with simultaneously strong deviations of αs and βs from zero. Figure 13 also highlights that the other models do not benefit from these additional degrees of freedom in terms of their ability to reduce the tension.

Finally, it is worth pointing out that the αs/βs solutions preferred here do not significantly alter the constraints on S8 – without αs/βs , the average S8 is 0.829, while with αs/βs the average is S8 is 0.826. The shift is small compared to the average uncertainty of 0.007. However, the small-scale sensitivity of galaxy clustering [216, 234, 235] and the Lyman-α forest [236–241] on models with an enhancement or suppression of the power spectrum could restrict these models further. We leave a dedicated analysis for future work.

G. Selection of finalists

Let us recall that we select the finalist models according to thresholds defined in section III C, which require a significant improvement in the combined fit (with the MB prior). A model passes to the knockout round whenever −∆AIC > 10 or ln BF > 3.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
It is clear from section IV and especially section IV B that group E models outperform other groups according to the model preference metrics. The varying electron mass model from group M is the only other model which barely passes the thresholds. Finally, no models in groups R, L, or E+L pass the threshold. Nevertheless, we have seen in section IV E and fig. 11 that group R models would pass the thresholds in absence of ACT data or when supplemented with a running of the power spectrum. To illustrate how they perform in the additional tests of the knockout round, we select as a ‘wild card’ and for reference, the best-performing model from this group, which is the WZDR model.

An important question that arises is whether the tests of the knockout round should be carried out on the finalist models considered only in their simplest form (with a cosmological constant and assuming flatness), or also in their extended versions (with CPL dark energy, spatial curvature, or a deviation from a power law primordial power spectrum). We decide to focus on models in their simplest form to reduce computational complexity. However, we make an exception for the “gold medal winner” of Ref. [13], the varying me model with curvature, which is shown for reference. Extended models that we mention as potential finalists but which are not included are the curved EMG and RnR models, as well as all group R models with αs/βs. Note that for all models, the ability to mitigate the Hubble tension remains unchanged when considering an evolving DE with a CPL parametrization.

Planck data until ℓ= 1800 in TT, ℓ= 1050 in TE, and ℓ= 600 in EE, cutting the ACT and SPT data correspondingly. These transition values are chosen such that Planck and ACT have roughly similar constraining power at the corresponding multipoles. Thus, this choice maximizes the overall constraining power from the CMB.

– In the ‘extended plik’ variation, we use the same transition multipoles as in the ‘ex-

tended CamSpec’ variation, but we replace the CamSpec likelihood by the plik one, marginalizing over all nuisance parameters with the priors described in Ref. [190].

• DES Y5 Dovekie: For uncalibrated SN data, we substitute Pantheon+ with the Dovekierecalibrated DES Y5 dataset [242].

• S8 prior: We add a Gaussian prior on S8 = 0.789 ± 0.012 corresponding to the result of the DES Y6 3x2pt photometric analysis [202].

• BBN: We use the PRyMordial code to compute the light element abundances in a grid of (Ωbh2, ∆Neff or mearly

e /mlate

e ) using either the PArthENoPE or PRIMAT reaction rates. These abundances are then compared to Ref. [243] which measures the deuterium fraction D/H = (2.527 ± 0.030) · 10−5 and Ref. [244] which measures the Helium abundance Yp = 0.2458 ± 0.0013. Similarly to Ref. [122], we set tau_n_flag=False and let the PRyMordial code self-consistently determine the neutron lifetime.

B. Extended Planck multipoles

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
section: The knockout round: additional tests on the finalist models
text:
The cuts in CMB multipoles in our baseline analysis of section IV B allow for easier comparison to previous literature such as Refs. [2, 3], but are not tuned to optimize the overall CMB constraining power. Indeed, they were chosen to include all ACT and/or SPT data and avoid covariance with Planck, which is hard to estimate. Here, instead, we attempt to build a combined CMB dataset that (approximately) maximizes constraining power. We do so by comparing the binned uncertainties from each experiment and choosing a multipole cut that approximately coincides with the transition from Planck-dominated to ground-based-experiment-dominated error bars, similarly to the approach of Ref. [245]. Consequently, these constraints incorporate more of the Planck CMB data compared to the baseline cuts.

In general, the constraints do not shift very significantly, as shown in figs. 15 and 16. Between the baseline and ‘extended CamSpec’ analysis, the tension level fluctuates by at most ±0.4σ. All models except for the WZDR and Varying me(+Ωk) models see an increase in the tension by about 0.2σ, consistent with an increase in the constraining power of the ‘extended CamSpec’ compared to the ‘baseline’ configuration. Instead, the WZDR model shows a decrease in the tension from 4.5σ to 4.1σ in MB, consistent with the preference in ACT data against a large Nwzdr, while the Varying me(+Ωk) model also shows a reduction from 4.1σ to 3.6σ.

The ‘extended plik’ configuration, on the other hand, decreases the tension almost universally (by roughly −0.5σ), with the only exception being the NEDE model, for which the tension increases slightly. As before, the WZDR and Varying me(+Ωk) models show the largest change (−0.6σ and −1.1σ, respectively), though the EMG model and the varying me model also see a significant decrease in the tension (both −0.4σ).

C. DES-Dovekie supernovae

In our baseline analysis we employ the Pantheon+ SNeIa compilation. While the impact of the SN compilation on the final constraints is less than that of the CMB or BAO data, the use of different SN compilations or analysis pipelines can in principle alter our conclusions.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
section: The knockout round: additional tests on the finalist models
text:
This is because the SNeIa datasets have an impact mainly as an additional probe of the fractional matter density Ωm. In particular, they prefer slightly larger values than CMB and DESI BAO data. Given that the Ωm parameter is impacted differently by the competing models, SNeIa data can be quite important for model selection. For example, the initial analysis of the DES Y5 dataset in Ref. [246] found comparatively higher values of Ωm = 0.352 ± 0.017 (68%) in ΛCDM than the Pantheon+ value Ωm = 0.334 ± 0.018. Instead, the recent DES Dovekie reanalysis of Ref. [242] found that an improved photometric cross-calibration and a retraining of the light-curve model yield smaller values, Ωm = 0.330 ± 0.015, in better agreement with Pantheon+. The DES Dovekie error bar is however smaller, restricting both low and high values of Ωm.

Due to parameter degeneracies (e.g. Refs. [113, 119]), there is a systematic trend of models from group M to reach high values of H0 only at the expense of significantly lowering Ωm . The trend is less pronounced for models from groups E and R. We thus expect the switch from Pantheon+ to DES Dovekie data to cut into the region of parameter space of group M models with the lowest Ωm , and to limit their ability to reduce the Hubble tension.

Our results are shown in fig. 17. As expected, the varying-electron-mass model is noticeably affected by the DES Dovekie SN data, since it produces the largest reduction in Ωm. Nevertheless, the effect remains small, shifting the constraints from H0 = (69.10+0.71

D. Neutrino mass prior

In the baseline analysis presented in section IV G, we have used a flat prior on the neutrino mass sum that requires it to be larger than 0. However, values of P mν below 58 meV are already in > 2σ tension with neutrino oscillation experiments even assuming normal mass ordering [247]. Since in many cases the sum of neutrino masses correlates with other parameters, in particular H0 and extended model parameters, it is crucial to investigate whether an oscillation-motivated prior changes the ability of these models to reduce the Hubble tension.

We thus repeat our CMB+BAO+SN analysis with a new prior P mν ≥58 meV. The results are summarized in fig. 18. Also in this case, the new results do not depart significantly from those of the baseline analysis. The tension level in MB remains very stable for most models, and decreases at most by −0.2σ for the WZDR, NEDE, and varying me models. Exceptionally, the Varying me(+Ωk) model shows a reduction of the tension by −1.4σ in this case, down to 2.9σ, making it competitive with group E models in this case.

E. Baryonic feedback

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
section: The knockout round: additional tests on the finalist models
text:
Non-linear structure formation affects the high-ℓCMB lensing power spectrum and therefore the lensed TT,TE,EE power spectra. It is thus very relevant for analyses performed in this work, given the large multipole range considered here. One important question is whether the impact of high-ℓdamping-tail measurements on the Hubble tension, already discussed in sections IV E and IV F, might be affected by the details of non-linear modeling. For this purpose, we investigate the consequence of marginalizing over the parameter TAGN of HMcode 2020 [248], which provides a proxy for the amplitude of baryonic feedback effects on the non-linear matter spectrum (baryonic feedback was neglected in the baseline analysis). We show the impact of this marginalization on the main model parameters in fig. 19. No significant deviation is found with respect to the baseline analysis, and according to fig. 14 the tension level does not fluctuate by more than ±0.2σ. This is consistent with the expectation that the uncertainty of current CMB experiments is sufficient to necessitate a non-linear treatment of the CMB lensing power spectrum, but not to distinguish between different baryonic feedback models, as illustrated in Refs. [123, 249]. Notably, while much larger ranges of σi/Mpl are allowed for the EMG model, this does not result in much wider contours for H0 , reducing the tension in H0 only by ∼−0.3σ.

F. Clustering amplitude S8

As is well known (e.g. [124, 207]), models resolving the Hubble tension can lead to a larger S8, in particular those in group E [83–87, 250], as was discussed in section IV. In this section we investigate the impact of data constraining S8 on the ability of finalist models to reduce the Hubble tension. For this purpose, we use the combined S8 measurement from the DES-Y6 3x2pt analysis11 [202], S8 = 0.789 ± 0.012, which is the tightest currently available measurement of the clustering of matter. For simplicity, we treat the S8 parameter derived under ΛCDM from the full analysis as a Gaussian likelihood. The resulting constraints are shown in fig. 20. As expected, most of group E models are more constrained once S8 data are included and, according to table X, the tension level in MB raises by up to 0.7σ for these models (for H0 only +0.3σ). Instead, the WZDR model from group R is unaffected, and the varying electron mass model from group M actually performs better (−0.3σ), in particular once curvature is included (−1.4σ, down to 2.7σ tension). We already mentioned that models from group M ease the tension at the expense of smaller values of Ωm, which naturally lead to a smaller S8 = σ8

G. Big Bang Nucleosynthesis constraints

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
section: The knockout round: additional tests on the finalist models
text:
Finally, we investigate whether the addition of BBN constraints coming from the measurement of light element abundances significantly impact our results. It has been pointed out already in Ref. [201] and Ref. [122] that the Ωbh2 constraints provided by deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio measurements can significantly affect models that ease the Hubble tension. The degeneracies exploited by group E models typically favor higher values of Ωbh2, potentially bringing them into tension with BBN constraints.

Since the EMG model involves non-trivial modifications of gravitational couplings even at early times relevant for nucleosynthesis, specific modifications of BBN theory codes are required to accurately predict primordial element abundances in this case. This goes beyond the scope of our work. Thus, we exclude the EMG and Thawing Gravity models from this analysis, but note that tight bounds such as those derived in Ref. [252] are likely to apply also here.

There are currently two main approaches to model the BBN nuclear reaction rates, exemplified in the PArthENoPE [253, 254] and PRIMAT [255, 256] codes. As these are known to yield significantly different values for the deuterium fraction, we perform two sets of analyses, using either models.

11 We expect that using KiDS legacy results with S8 = 0.815+0.016 −0.021 [251] instead would lead to constraints closer to the baseline analyses presented previously.

text:
We find that regardless of the code used, the parameter constraints are significantly stronger than in the baseline analysis for all the finalist models. With the PArthENoPE rates (see fig. 21), the level of tension increases by +0.5σ in MB uniformly. With the PRIMAT rates (see fig. 22), Ωbh2

is constrained to lower values by primordial deuterium measurements (resulting in a ∼2σ tension with the baryon density inferred from Planck in ΛCDM). This further strengthens the parameter constraints and increases the tension level for all group E models – for instance, by +0.7σ for NEDE, while causing a ∼+0.4σ overall tension level increase for the other models.

H. Summary of the knockout round

The knockout round allowed us to check the robustness of our main results against several relevant variations in data and assumptions, summarized in table X. The overall conclusion is that the baseline results of the group stage analysis are extremely stable, with the most significant change coming from the inclusion of BBN constraints or the inclusion of an S8 prior from DES Y6 3x2pt data. BBN constraints universally worsen the outcomes (increasing the tension in MB by about ∼0.4 −0.7σ), while the S8 constraints raise the tension strongly for group E models (by around +0.5σ) but reduce the tension for the varying me model (−0.3σ and −1.4σ with curvature), making the curved varying me model competitive with group E in this case. The curved varying me model also has a strong reduction in tension when a physical prior on the neutrino mass is imposed, by −1.2σ. In most other cases studied here, the tension level typically varies by at most ±0.3σ.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text: Using current CMB, BAO, and Type Ia supernova data, we have compared fourteen proposed solutions to the Hubble tension with a common analysis framework, which we dub the “H0 World Cup”. The contenders are representative of five broad categories: models with late-time modifications of the background evolution (group L), modifications of recombination (group M), additional radiation before recombination (group R), and early dark energy injection or early modified gravity (group E). We have assessed the performance of each model using complementary Frequentist and Bayesian measures of both the residual tension and the improvement in the fit relative to ΛCDM. The two statistical approaches yield a broadly consistent ranking, and models based on the same physical mechanism generally exhibit similar performance.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
This work builds upon the original “H0 Olympics” which established a common framework for benchmarking proposed solutions using the cosmological data and model implementations then available [13]. This approach was already updated in Ref. [15] with newer CMB and BAO data (ACT-DR4, SPT-3G 2018, eBOSS). The current work uses even more recent and constraining data in its baseline analysis (ACT-DR6, SPT-3G D1, DESI DR2, Pantheon+) and in the extended analyses of section V (DES Y5 Dovekie, DES Y6 3x2pt, recent primordial abundances). It incorporates additional models and mechanisms proposed recently. It complements the Frequentist criteria of Ref. [13] with Bayesian parameter-shift and model-evidence metrics. It systematically tests the impact of curvature, CPL dark energy, and a free neutrino mass, before subjecting the finalists to dedicated robustness tests involving alternative CMB likelihoods and multipole cuts, supernova samples, large-scale-structure information, and BBN.

As in the original analysis, the models considered here should be understood primarily as representative of phenomenological mechanisms rather than as complete fundamental theories, since several of them lack a compelling particle-physics embedding or a known ultraviolet completion. Our updated ranking therefore identifies promising physical directions and clarifies which conclusions depend on particular datasets or analysis choices; it should not be interpreted as evidence that any specific implementation is the correct theory.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
Baseline competition. For our baseline CMB+BAO+SN dataset, ΛCDM exhibits a discrepancy above 5.5σ in the supernova calibration parameter MB. We use MB, rather than H0 alone, because it consistently incorporates the calibration information while accounting for the small Ωm tension emerging between CMB, DESI BAO, and uncalibrated supernova data. The main baseline results, summarized in tables II to VI, are:

• Group E gives the best overall performance. These models reduce the residual tension to approximately 3σ and are strongly favored over ΛCDM by the model-comparison metrics.

• Group M provides an intermediate improvement. Its best-performing model reduces the residual tension to approximately 4σ and receives moderate support relative to ΛCDM.

• Group R performs only marginally better than ΛCDM. Its best model leaves a residual tension of approximately 4.5σ, with little or no model-comparison preference over ΛCDM.

• Groups L and E+L perform worst overall. The late-time and mixed late+early-time models considered here do not significantly reduce the tension once confronted with the full baseline dataset.

45

The DESI DR2 BAO data adds significant constraining power on Ωm for all models and tend to shift the contours in a direction beneficial to the Hubble tension, except for the iDM-DE and Varying me models. Apart from H0 and Ωm, the standard cosmological parameters have stable constraints under the inclusion of new physics, with the exception of the summed neutrino mass which may reach higher values in the Varying me model or in the Agnos. Reion. case.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
Comparison with H0 Olympics results. The updated ranking differs most clearly for groups R and M. Radiation-based solutions, which remained viable in the previous competition, are no longer competitive in the baseline analysis and do not meet the thresholds to be selected as finalists. The WZDR model is retained in the knockout round only as a reference. The Varying me model also performs substantially worse than in the original Olympics and barely passes the threshold to be among the finalists. These changes are driven primarily by the inclusion of ACT DR6 data, which tightly constrain the CMB signatures produced by these mechanisms.

As a matter of fact, we have checked that removing ACT substantially changes the relative ranking and improves the Bayes factor almost universally. In the no-ACT analysis, most models in groups R, M, and E reduce the residual tension to approximately 3–3.5σ and achieve comparable Bayesian model preferences; cold NEDE reaches approximately 2.3σ. ACT data are therefore central to the stronger baseline constraints on groups R and M and to the clearer preference for group E.

Extension of each model. Next, we have tested whether adding late-time freedom to each contender in the form of spatial curvature or CPL dark energy changes the ranking:

• Spatial curvature has little impact on most models. The clearest improvement occurs for group M models and the Rock-n-Roll model, which benefit from the additional freedom in the angular-diameter distance and from the weaker late-time determination of Ωm when curvature is allowed.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
• CPL dark energy does not improve the ability of the models to reach the local calibration from SH0ES. Variations in (w0, wa) generally counteract the pre-recombination modifications and shift the inferred H0 downward. However, introducing models that ease the Hubble tension tends to reduce the preference for a departure from a cosmological constant. This reduction is strongest for Varying me and WZDR, while the Agnos. Reion. case yields the broadest constraints.

• A deviation from a power-law primordial power spectrum, parametrized by αs and βs , strongly improves the performance of all group R models as well the varying electron mass model. This is because of the role that ACT plays in severely constraining those models. We find a preference for αs̸ = 0 and βs̸ = 0, in agreement with Ref. [224], and a reduction of the Hubble tension to the 3 −3.5σ level.

Robustness of the finalists. After selecting the best-performing baseline models, we subject them to the additional tests described in section V. The main conclusions are:

• CMB likelihoods: the overall conclusions are stable over the studied variations, although the plik likelihood is generally more permissive than CamSpec. WZDR and varying me(+Ωk) benefit the most from shifting the transition from Planck to ACT data to higher multipoles, consistent with the strong ACT constraints on dark-radiation models. Allowing for baryonic feedback effects in the nonlinear modeling of CMB lensing does not significantly alter the constraints.

46

• Supernova samples: the tighter Ωm constraint from the Dovekie-recalibrated DES Y5 sample weakens the constraints on the Varying me model by a very small amount, but has a negligible impact on the other finalists.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
• Neutrino-mass prior: imposing the lower bound on Σmν motivated by the normal hierarchy shifts most models toward slightly higher H0, with the exceptions of EDE and ΛCDM. The strongest shift is seen for the varying me(+Ωk) model, making it competitive with group E models in this case.

• Clustering amplitude: adding the DES Y6 S8 constraint weakens group E solutions because their increase in H0 is generally accompanied by a larger S8 . WZDR is nearly unaffected, whereas Varying me benefits mildly and Varying me(+Ωk) strongly from the additional constraint because its lower preferred Ωm also lowers S8 . A complete assessment including full-shape large-scale-structure information is left for future work.

• BBN constraints: light-element abundances can restrict models in groups R, M, and E, but the strength of this conclusion depends somewhat on whether the PArthENoPE or PRIMAT nuclear reaction rates are adopted. Nuclear-rate uncertainties therefore remain an important caveat when assessing these models.

title: The $H_0$ world cup. II. A comprehensive competition between proposed Hubble tension solutions
text:
Overall, no model fully resolves the Hubble tension in the full baseline analysis, but the comparison reveals a clear hierarchy among physical mechanisms: early dark energy injection (minimally and non-minimally coupled to gravity) currently performs the best, while recombination and darkradiation solutions remain more sensitive to the choice of CMB and low-redshift datasets. The ranking is robust to several analysis choices, but S8 and BBN information expose important complementary tests and theoretical challenges. Deviations from a pure power-law primordial power spectrum substantially improve the ability of models with extra radiation (group R) or a varying electron mass to address the tension, bringing them close to the performance of group E models. A varying electron mass model also benefits from curvature, although not as substantially as previously found. Progress will require continued scrutiny of observational systematics, to strengthen the underlying theoretical basis of many proposed mechanisms, and to look for new mechanisms that can ease multiple tensions simultaneously. The time is ripe for revolutionary models in cosmology and the search for a solution beyond the ΛCDM cosmological standard model is now more important than ever.

D. Nuisance parameter correlation

In figs. 28 to 31 we show the 68% and 95% CL contours showing the correlation between the cosmological parameters and the nuisance parameters of the Planck CamSpec and lite ACT and SPT likelihoods discussed in section IV A. We see that there are no very strong correlations. The strongest one is between the EE calibration parameters and the scalar tilt ns in the 4-parameter modified recombination model.
